#2079. “Cashing in” on Castellanos claim ignores one major stumbling block | West Ham News

Ever since the closing days of the summer transfer window there have been claims that West Ham will be cashing in on Taty Castellanos in the winter: The Argentine has been a huge disappointment in the 15 games of West Ham’s championship season, with just a solitary goal to show for his efforts.

At times he’s resembled more of a moody, disinterested bystander and seems pretty much the most likely player in the eleven to be yellow carded each time he plays.

A solitary goal is plain unacceptable for the frontman who cost £27 million: Claims that he’ll be sold in the winter abound.

Sadly, Everton’s late interest in the summer window, reportedly around £40 million, appears to have evaporated as Taty’s form has waned. Understandably.

Far from happy: One goal in fifteen means Castellanos has been a huge let down in the second tier. Its also means those big money suitors have now evaporated

The newest suggestions from EFL specialist site the72.co.uk suggest Castellanos could be heading back home – however there’s a catch:

“River Plate reportedly view the 28-year-old as a priority target in their striker search, although the finances involved in the deal could prove to be a major hurdle. However, cashing in could give WHUFC the chance to sign a true talisman to aid their promotion bid. “

“Cashing in”? I think not: That’s the elephant in the room here. River Plate have already disclosed that they’ll look at some kind of loan or shared purchase option – as they’re short of funds – which of course will cut no ice with West Ham who will want to replace Taty with a striker more suited to scoring the Championship goals they require.

Merely shipping Taty out on loan without a permanent sale will serve no useful purpose and could actually weaken Scott Parker’s squad. The Hammers have enough loaned – out unwanted stars as it is: Another one added to the list won’t help a rebuild. The only possible route could involve a swap for goal keeper Santiago Beltran – which would still leave the Hammers short of a goal scorer and needing to offload Hermansen or Areola in the winter.

And how often to these player swaps ever come off? Exactly.

#2078. Alan Shearer explains why Ezri Konsa has impressed him

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Alan Shearer believes Ezri Konsa has been the Premier League’s best player this season after an impressive start to his Arsenal career.

But the former Newcastle United striker has been impressed by the Gunners’ backline and feels Konsa should take a large amount of credit for the fact that they have not missed William Saliba so much.

Konsa’s arrival at Emirates has provided Mikel Arteta with a defender, but his performances have caused some issues for the Arsenal boss. Konsa is now a viable option for Arteta to play, as Saliba is fit again.

Shearer feels Konsa has done enough to be regarded as the best player in the division so far.

He stated in the Metro that Konsa has been effective while playing for Arsenal in the defence.

The former Newcastle player believed that Konsa has been the best player in the Premier League during this season. He pointed out the proof of the performance in the defence, arguing that people did not notice the missing Saliba until now.

Konsa has proved just how much he has grown since moving to the Emirates. Arsenal have been very strong at the back with Konsa playing a massive part.

But there is a problem with Konsa’s performances. Even if Saliba is fit he has done more than enough to make his place difficult to take.

Saliba is still one of Arsenal’s most important defenders, so Arteta will be delighted to have him back. However, he can’t ignore what Konsa has done in his absence.

It would be a tough call to leave the Englishman out, as he has been in such great form. But it means an experienced first choice defender would be left on the bench.

Konsa and Saliba could make a good partnership if they are given time to understand each other on the pitch. They will need to play regularly to do this.

Konsa has made it very hard not to pick him. He has been performing so well that he has created a dilemma for the manager.

Shearer highlights how well he has done by saying this. Arteta will have to figure out how to make the most out of his two quality defenders.

Transfer stories have leapt with the arrival of new head coach Scott Parker – each manager has his own ideas on the ideal shape of his squad and Parker’s preferences will be very different to those of his predecessor. Matt’s article this morning dealt with the suggestion that Parker’s former defender CJ Egan Riley could be a January target.

Last week – largely un-noticed during the noise of Parker’s appointment and West Ham’s two Championship fixtures, flashscore reported that Scott Parker’s priority in January could well be to set up a reunion with former defensive midfielder Harrison Reed. But knowing how managers each have their own ‘pet’ players – such as Nuno with Traore and Morato – experience tells us that it could well be a transfer story that gathers pace as the winter window nears. If he has half the impact of Kevin Nolan, he’ll be very welcome indeed.

#2076. Why England fans booed Arsenal defender Ben White again after Croatia win

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Ben White returned to the England senior squad on Thursday night but received a hostile reception at Wembley.

The Arsenal defender came on as a substitute in the 78th minute of England’s 2-1 Nations League win against Croatia but was met with boos from a section of the crowd.

Thomas Tuchel has since defended White, stating that he should be in the squad. However, this raises questions as to why some England supporters have turned on the defender after he has continued to perform well for Arsenal.

The answer lies with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

He did not play in the first two group games for England and missed the last group game against Wales due to illness.

There were reports that White had fallen out with assistant manager Steve Holland, but neither the FA nor England management confirmed this was the reason he left.

Gareth Southgate later stated there were no problems between White and Holland and that White had simply withdrawn himself from selection after the tournament.

This meant that White would never play for England again while Southgate was still manager. Some fans were clearly upset by this, as they felt White was shunning his country.

When White returned under Tuchel in March 2026, he was met with a negative reaction. He was booed by the crowd when he scored his first-ever international goal against Uruguay. White was also booed in the same fashion against Japan.

He has since explained that supporters might view the situation differently if they knew the full story. However, he has chosen not to reveal the private details behind his departure.

Tuchel has shown little concern about White being affected by the controversy.

The England boss said after the win on Thursday that he had not heard any boos and praised White’s qualities, work ethic and desire to play for his country.

He believes White can help England win games and added that he has the backing of the coaching staff.

Arsenal fans will be unsurprised to learn that White is still a valuable asset for Mikel Arteta, offering defensive consistency and being able to play as a right or centre-back.

The bad press that White is receiving from England fans will not go away any time soon. However, he has not done anything to hurt his reputation at club level. The reasons why he left for the World Cup are personal.

The main focus for Arsenal will be getting him match fit again. As for the England fans, we shall see.

#2075. The one key question on which nearly all West Ham fans are in agreement

It is not often that West Ham fans appear unified over anything, after recent seasons of strife, division, disagreement and dispute with the Sullivan and Brady leadership, it feels as if ‘disharmony’ has been the default setting.

Not, it seems, about everything. There is one hot topic on which a huge majority of West Ham fans are in almost total agreement.

According to the NY Times’ fan survey, the biggest consensus was not for the approval of the new manager – although there is a pretty strong 77% majority of fans who responded who give the appointment of Scott Parker the thumbs up.

The biggest single factor on which most West Ham supporters agree is the choice of goalkeeper. According to the survey:

“Of the fans surveyed, an overwhelming 85.4 per cent believe Alphonse Areola should reclaim the No 1 jersey from Mads Hermansen.

Likeable yes, dependable no: 85% of West Ham fans want Hermansen out of the team

Interestingly, though, a sizeable 62 per cent of supporters believe the travelling contingent at Ewood Park were not right to boo Hermansen.”

Eighty five percent of fans have had enough of the Dane’s inept performances in between the sticks, with one fan driven to comment that West Ham’s goal would be better defended simply by hanging a green jersey on the cross bar rather than continuing to select the out of form Hermansen.

Of course the fly in the ointment is that Areola has been reported as ‘unfit’ – whether that means third choice Finlay Herrick comes into consideration – who can say- but it’d be a brave selection for Parker to leave his number one on the bench if Areola isn’t ready for the Preston North End fixture next weekend, however much it seems supporters want to see Hermansen out of the team.

#2074. Steven Gerrard explains his theory on why Alexis Mac Allister has been so resurgent this season

Steven Gerrard has offered a theory as to why Alexis Mac Allister has looked so resurgent this season compared to last.

The midfielder was one of the Reds’ most disappinting players of a dreadful 2025/26 campaign, especially having been such a key component in the preceding Premier League title triumph, but he’s been playing near to his best since Andoni Iraola took charge in the summer.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily (via Liverpool Echo), our former captain claimed that the 27-year-old subconsciously let his performance levels drop last season as he was privately consumed by trying to retain the World Cup with Argentina.

Gerrard said of Mac Allister: “I’ve loved him this season. I think last year, like a lot of the Argentinian players, they had a bit of a distraction with the World Cup coming up.

“It’s the way they are. The World Cup takes over everything in their lives, and I lived that with Emiliano Martínez when I was at Aston Villa. I just think it becomes a priority.

“I think it becomes a bit of a distraction. It becomes the most important thing in their lives, to be ready and not injured and make sure that the national team is the priority.

“I think with a lot of the Argentina players, I’m sure a lot of managers, if they watch this, will say: ‘Yeah, I’ve experienced that.’”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

It’s an interesting theory that Gerrard has put forward to explain why Mac Allister’s performances from last season to this have been so chalk and cheese.

Many footballers consider the World Cup as the pinnacle of their careers, and the Liverpool midfielder represents a nation where the sport is nothing short of an obsession.

Only the 27-year-old could truthfully answer whether or not he let his levels dip in 2025/26 because he was prioritising the global tournament in North America, but from a Reds perspective we’d hope that isn’t the case.

As a player employed by LFC, Mac Allister has a duty to give full commitment to representing the club. As disappointing as his performances were last season, though, we wouldn’t go as far as accusing him of not giving less than 100%, which’d be a serious indictment of an elite footballer.

Thankfully, the Argentine has looked much more like his usual self since August, to the point where Troy Deeney suggested that he would even inspire Liverpool to nudge their way into the Premier League title race if he maintains or improves further upon his current standards.

The 27-year-old has been vocal about his contract situation at Anfield, but if he keeps playing the way that he has been, securing a new deal for him should become a matter of priority for sporting director Richard Hughes.

#2073. Arsenal Women vs London City Lionesses preview: Gunners face tough test at the Emirates

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal look to build on their recent win over Liverpool as they return to the Emirates Stadium but will face an impressive London City Lionesses side who are a potent attacking threat on their travels.

Renée Slegers’ team have struggled to convert their strong performances into points in the league this season. They have lost their last four WSL games at home, however, becoming the first team in WSL history to draw four successive games at home.

Their bad run must come to an end. They have taken just three points from their first nine league games so far this season, scoring a miserable total of 10 goals. However, they look like they have more in the tank and will need to be much more clinical in front of the goal.

The day also marks Slegers’ 50th game in charge of the WSL. The Dutch manager has only lost six league games so far this season, with only Chelsea having a better record from teams that have been ever-present in the division.

Arsenal can’t take their opposition lightly after London City’s impressive recent form. They have won two and drawn once in their last three away league games, scoring 12 goals.

Eder Maestre’s side has become a potent attacking force. Daniëlle van de Donk has provided four assists this season, and Delphine Cascarino has scored three goals and provided two assists.

Kadidiatou Diani can be dangerous. She has scored or assisted in all four of her league games away from home this season.

London City’s attacking prowess means they are a far different proposition to some teams Arsenal have faced at home. They have been in a positive situation for 62.7 per cent of their league minutes this season, the highest in the WSL.

Arsenal will have to deal with the attacking threats but look to utilise their ball possession better. Giving London City an opportunity to counter could make an already tough afternoon even tougher.

Alessia Russo comes into the game having found the net in her last three WSL games and will be key in converting Arsenal’s chances into goals.

The Gunners also showed their fighting spirit in their midweek clash against Barcelona. They drew 1-1 at Camp Nou to become the first side to take points off the Spanish giants in the Women’s Champions League at home since April 2024.

Slegers’ team will feel emboldened by that result but will have to change their tactics against London City.

They have won all seven games against Arsenal so far, scoring an impressive 22 goals and only conceding once. However, given London City’s recent away form, they will be hotly favoured.

They certainly have the quality to take all three points, but they must finally convert their dominance into a comfortable home win.

#2070. Arsenal transfer interest in Alphadjo Cisse: Arsenal face a £50m decision as AC Milan youngster attracts Premier League interest

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal transfer interest in Alphadjo Cisse is starting to take shape. Arsenal are monitoring the development of AC Milan starlet Alphadjo Cissé, although his sensational start to the season could prove to be costly for Mikel Arteta.

The 20-year-old has made a blistering start to his Serie A career and attracted interest from a number of Premier League clubs after his impressive displays so far. Arsenal are reported to be interested.

The Gunners are among several clubs, including Brighton, keeping tabs on the player, according to Italian football news website Tuttomercatoweb. The striker is rumoured to be worth up to 60 million euros. That’s an eye-watering sum for a player who is just starting out in his professional career.

Cissé was signed by Milan from Hellas Verona in February 2026 but was allowed to finish the season on loan at Catanzaro.

Prior to joining the San Siro, he had already showcased his potential with six goals in 22 games in Serie B. He has made a huge impact since moving up to the top division.

Cissé has found the net five times in nine Serie A games this season. He has also chipped in with three goals in four Europa League games, making a total of eight goals in 13 games.

This has made him an important addition to the Milan squad. He is also versatile, as he can play as an attacking midfielder or higher up the park.

Arsenal may find his versatility attractive. Arteta likes players who can play in different positions and with injuries, and with a busy fixture list, he will want to have players who can do that.

The main issue could be that Milan are keen to keep their young star.

It is reported that the Italian club have turned down a verbal offer from Brighton and are looking to extend Cissé’s contract, which currently runs until June 2030.

This indicates that Milan is considering his future, rather than looking to make a profit. It also demonstrates just how quickly his reputation has developed.

Arsenal have the funds to target exciting young talent, but would they want to spend so much on Cissé?

There is no indication that he would be an instant replacement for Arsenal’s current attacking options. However, Cissé’s age, goal-scoring ability and versatility make him an interesting prospect.

This could be one to keep an eye on beyond January. Milan have little motivation to sell, and Arsenal might want to see how he develops before committing themselves.

Cissé has already hit the ground running in Italy and now needs to prove that his initial success can turn into something more consistent.

#2068. Max Dowman breaks Jude Bellingham record as Arsenal teenager makes England history

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Max Dowman has added another incredible achievement to his burgeoning career after becoming the youngest player to play for the England Under-21s.

The Arsenal youngster was introduced from the bench in Friday’s 1-0 friendly loss to Portugal at Ashton Gate. The 16-year-10-month-13-day-old player is over three months younger than Jude Bellingham was when he played his first game for the Under-21s.

Dowman replaced former Arsenal academy player Amario Cozier-Duberry in the 61st minute. He came on alongside debutant Trey Nyoni as England tried to shift the momentum of a challenging game.

An early strike from Afonso Moreira gave Portugal the lead in the 28th minute. An ineffective England team failed to respond. However, the replacements gave Lee Carsley’s team some late momentum.

Despite the hosts’ attempts to level the score, they failed to break down the Portuguese defence. The result means England have lost for the second game running. However, Dowman had much to be pleased with personally.

Dowman has added to his growing collection of records.

He became the youngest player to play in the Champions League, the youngest goalscorer in the history of the Premier League and the youngest to win the Premier League title.

Breaking Bellingham’s England Under-21 record is another significant step. It shows how quickly Dowman has progressed through the international age groups.

He has already made a big impression at Arsenal with Mikel Arteta’s love of giving younger players a chance, but Dowman will have some stiff competition for first team minutes.

Another positive is his progression on an international scale. He will improve both physically and tactically playing against older players and gain experience at a higher level.

England will host France in their next friendly on Monday, 16th November. Dowman will be hoping to feature after his instant impact on the record books.

Despite the disappointing result against Portugal, it was a landmark evening for the Arsenal players.

Dowman is already building a legacy at club level, but now he can add to his list of records by becoming an England Under-21 record holder.

At just 16, he has plenty of time to improve and show consistent performances to get more opportunities with the senior Arsenal squad.

#2066. James Pearce claim seems to pour cold water over Liverpool links with Finn Jeltsch

Liverpool, it’s fair to say, have a pretty active recruiting department.

A necessarily active recruiting department, it should be emphasised, given the squad-building challenges Andoni Iraola has already faced early on in his tenure as head coach.

The Merseysiders navigated a potential centre-back crisis expertly in the summer with the arrival of loan signing Ronald Araujo from Barcelona. But questions remain as to the long-term viability of the centre-back department post the summer 2027 transfer window.

A recent report from Christian Falk with CF Bayern Insider asserted that Liverpool, among Europe’s elite, have scouted VfB Stuttgart centre-back Finn Jeltsch.

“It is TRUE: Liverpool have scouted VfB Stuttgart centre-back Finn Jeltsch. All the top clubs, including Bayern Munich, are scouting him,” the head of football at Bild said.

“He was in the squad for Klopp first as a backup for the right-back. Then one of the central defenders became injured, and now he’s also the backup at centre-back. This shows he can play many positions, and everyone can see the 20-year-old’s potential.

“Such players really are a present to everyone. Jeltsch is young, talented and can play many positions, and he’s not so expensive! Bayern Munich has an eye on him.”

If that name seems vaguely familiar, it might be because Bundesliga giants Bayern Munich are already big fans of the footballer and are keeping a very close eye on matters close to home.

Liverpool’s interest is understandable. Come the summer transfer window, they could be two centre-halves down should Joe Gomez and Virgil van Dijk call time on their Anfield careers once their contracts run out. Ronald Araujo, though enjoying an impeccable campaign with the Reds, may not become a permanent addition to the squad, despite Liverpool possessing a buy option. Much here may depend on what Barcelona’s stance on the Uruguayan international looks like in May.

That’s three centre-backs Liverpool could be short come the opening of the summer transfer window, so it’s very plausible that Julian Ward and Co. will be keeping a close eye on the centre-back market between now and the end of the 2026/27 season.

As James Pearce rightly notes on X (formerly Twitter), of course, Liverpool do have several high-potential, highly exciting young centre-backs in their stable.

Ifeanyi Ndukwe, by all accounts, is impressing on loan at Levante after an eye-catching pre-season; Giovanni Leoni remains an appetising option, and then there’s hope for young Mor Talla Ndiaye also.

Centre-back not a priority for Liverpool so highly unlikely they will invest heavily in that area either in Jan or next summer. Jacquet has made a huge impact and big hopes for fellow young CBs Leoni, Ndukwe and Ndiaye.

— James Pearce (@JamesPearceLFC) November 13, 2026

But these are three very young, very inexperienced centre-backs you’d be pairing with the also youthful, but extremely impressive, Jeremy Jacquet for the foreseeable future. The Frenchman will, however, have a season of Premier League football under his belt – but is that enough to help guide the next generation of Liverpool centre-backs?

Unless you’re planning to extend Van Dijk’s contract or activate Araujo’s buy option, Liverpool are looking incredibly short on options with experience and genuine leadership credentials at L4.

That might be worth considering if the plan isn’t to invest in Finn Jeltsch this summer.

#2065. Martin Ødegaard sends clear message to Arsenal amid Bayern Munich transfer rumours

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Martin Ødegaard has spoken out about the speculation surrounding his future. He has stated he would like to stay at Arsenal for the future.

The captain has also admitted that talks about a new deal have not yet begun. Ødegaard is currently under contract until the summer of 2028. This leaves Arsenal with an important decision to make over the coming months.

Bayern Munich are being linked with an interest in the midfielder according to reports from Germany. The Bundesliga giants are said to be keeping their eyes on the player’s situation.

Speaking while on international duty with Norway, Ødegaard was quick to dismiss the speculation. He made it clear he is settled in north London and sees his future being at the Emirates Stadium.

There is no suggestion that the 27-year-old is seeking a move. Although comments do highlight a contract issue that Arsenal will be keen to resolve in the short term.

The Norwegian’s laid-back attitude should be encouraging for supporters.

He has made it clear that he is happy at the club and wants to stay here for the time being. This means that there is no need to panic.

However, Arsenal will have to get him to sign on the dotted line. Leaving his captain in the last year of his contract with no progress would cause an unnecessary distraction.

Since his permanent move from Real Madrid in 2021, Ødegaard has become a key player in Mikel Arteta’s plans. He has grown into a team leader and is one of the most influential players in the dressing room.

His importance has been shown by his inclusion in all 10 of Arsenal’s Premier League games so far this season. He has scored three goals.

This is a big improvement on last season, where he was hampered by injuries and failed to make much of an impact in front of goal.

It wouldn’t be a shock to see Bayern Munich show interest in Ødegaard, but don’t take this as a sign he is close to a move.

There is little reason for Arsenal to consider losing their captain. He brings so much more to the team than just his technical ability and has been relied upon by Arteta to lead by example.

The midfielder was also pivotal in the 1-0 win over Hull City on 7 November, scoring the winner in the 72nd minute to give the league leaders three crucial points.

Arsenal have put themselves in a good position in the title race. Keeping their key players happy will be important in the second half of the campaign.

The Gunners will be focused on their game against Newcastle United on 21st November.

Arsenal fans have no real reason to panic at the moment, with the captain wanting to stay at the club and his comments suggesting he is happy.

However, it would be a good idea for the club to try and ensure his long-term future at the club. Ødegaard is still an important part of Arteta’s strategy, and ensuring he stays at the club would be a smart move.

#2063. Liverpool tipped for January squad boost absolutely no one wants

Harvey Elliott is reportedly set to be sent packing back home to Liverpool in January.

That’s the claim coming out of the regional Valencian outlet Las Provincias (via Sport Witness), with the midfielder having only picked up 152 La Liga minutes out of a possible 810 on offer.

After some concerns were expressed over the former Fulham academy graduate having arrived overweight in the Spanish top-flight, it seems the 23-year-old has been unable to make any headway at Mestalla.

It’s worth noting that a permanent decision has yet to be made by the club, despite a string of concerns, but Elliott very much appears to be in the last-chance saloon. In fact, as relayed by Sport Witness: “If he does not improve in the coming weeks, the loan agreement with Liverpool could be terminated. They state that ‘talks will be held’.”

Not a lot of time for the footballer to buck up his ideas and earn himself a place in the hearts of the Valencia fans and, importantly, the decision-makers at the outfit.

It’s not looking great for Harvey Elliott, it has to be said.

After basically being iced out of the Liverpool squad by former Reds head coach Andoni Iraola, the playmaker was shipped off to Unai Emery’s Aston Villa and only picked up 284 minutes of action.

Mind, there seemed to be a weird kind of power play going on between Liverpool and the Villans, with the Reds unwilling to pay a significant amount of cash to cut the loan short and Emery’s side being apparently fine with letting a young player rot on the bench to make a point.

Point made. And now Elliott’s future is paying for it.

We do want to state, unequivocally, that we believe in Harvey Elliott and his potential. It wasn’t a million years ago when we were watching him thriving as part of Jurgen Klopp’s deep squad in the German’s final season in charge in 2023/24. But that season is becoming increasingly distant, and it’s becoming increasingly difficult to imagine Elliott ever playing a significant role for Liverpool again in future.

We hope he can turn things around in Valencia. Because if our No.19 comes back to L4 in January, it’s not an eventuality that will suit the player or the club at this stage.

#2062. Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.

The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes. Put simply, it measures which players are able to progress the ball through opposition lines while also contributing defensively.

The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.

The Championship’s elite midfielders increasingly occupy the top-right quadrant, combining progression and defensive intensity. That is why the chart identifies Norwich City’s Kenny McLean as one of the Championship’s most complete midfielders, posting outstanding line-breaking numbers while maintaining strong defensive output, despite only featuring for ten games out of fifteen due to an ankle injury.

Meanwhile, Portsmouth’s Ebou Adams is highlighted as a “defensive monster”, producing exceptional ball-winning statistics while still offering significant progression. Sheffield United’s Kalvin Phillips (yes the same player that flopped on loan at West Ham!), Queens Park Rangers’ Jonathan Varane and Norwich’s Jacob Wright also occupy impressive positions, demonstrating the ability to impact both sides of the game.

Mohamadou Kanté is viewed as a dynamic ball-carrying midfielder with strong physical attributes, but his game is built more around energy and transition play than elite progression metrics. Arne Engels offers technical quality and creativity, yet is generally more comfortable operating higher up the pitch than acting as a defensive controller.

The data is only based on players who have played an average of 540 mins so one omission is Tomas Souček, whose strengths have always been obvious. The Czech international on paper would arguably be the Championships most effective midfield goalscorer (3 in 7 appearances so far) and I’d expect him to feature highly for aerial presence. However, if plotted on a graph measuring line-breaking passes and ball-winning volume, he would likely owe more to his physicality and attacking threat than his ability to dictate possession through midfield.

That perhaps explains why West Ham can sometimes appear disconnected between defence and attack.

Too often there is a reliance on direct balls into attacking areas rather than building through the centre of the pitch. Equally, when possession is lost, the midfield does not always possess the combination of mobility and defensive output needed to regain control quickly.

West Ham arguably have midfielders who can create and win duels. What they appear to lack is a genuine “two-way” midfielder capable of consistently ranking highly in both categories.

That was precisely what Declan Rice offered during his time at the club. His ability to recover possession and immediately progress the ball remains incredibly difficult to replace.

The reality is Rice was never truly replaced, although finding a like-for-like successor was always going to be a near-impossible task

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse’s position on the chart is also interesting. A casualty of Nuno’s reign, he ranks among the highest players for line-breaking passes but has one of the lowest ball-winning outputs. Ward-Prowse excels at progressing possession but offers relatively little defensive contribution compared to the league’s most complete midfielders.

Above all the data serves as a reminder that Koppen’s recruitment and Parker’s existing choices for midfield should focus less on individual statistics and more on complete profiles.

Because the numbers suggest that is where Championship matches are increasingly won.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

I think there is nothing wrong with the Midfield. There is just a problem with the short pass mentality. The day of playing short passes across midfield are over in English football. You need decent long passes with good trapping and decent positive movement. How many of West Ham’s passes are square ball or back passes ? Far to many. Particularly back passes are all to often caught on to giving away needless goals. Walker-Peters is a really good example. Having moved forward beating someone, he then passes back in midfield, or worst still carries the ball backwards towards midfield or defence. Play positively, avoid back passes, learn to pass well and trap well and you have a very good midfield. Orford, Kante and other young players are far better at doing this, than the older players.

#2060. Ian Rush calls out bizarre Alexander Isak criticism after electric start rivals Haaland

Ian Rush has disagreed with the common consensus about Alexander Isak this season.

The Swedish international has been accused, at various times this season, of not being actively involved during Liverpool games.

As Rush was at pains to point out, the former Newcastle United hitman is scoring goals this season. Enough, at any rate, to put him in early contention with Manchester City’s Erling Haaland for the golden boot, with seven Premier League goals registered to the Norwegian’s nine – and in one fewer game to boot.

“People say that Isak isn’t getting involved much but he’s scoring goals and that’s all that matters. The hardest thing in football is to score a goal and he’s only second to (Erling) Haaland,” the Liverpool legend told BBC Sport.

It seems that no matter what the 27-year-old does in the famous red shirt, someone will have something negative to say about his performances.

But the fact remains that Isak is managing to get on the scoresheet with some degree of frequency as part of a frontline that is far from cohesive at this stage.

Can you imagine how many times he’ll be finding the back of the net once he finds a collective rhythm alongside Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola?

One may reasonably be inclined to think that critics have forgotten how Isak had the debut season from hell at Liverpool following his move from Newcastle in the summer.

The forward managed only 1,032 minutes across all competitions in Arne Slot’s final season in charge, between adductor issues and a broken fibula. 1,032 minutes, four goals and one assist. In 2026/27, the Swede has already racked up eight goals and an assist in 899 minutes of action (across all competitions).

Far easier for Alexander Isak to build fluency when he’s spending a lot more time on the pitch early in the season and stringing a series of starts together from one game to the next.

#2057. Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers1,2. However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples3, collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

Cancers develop through a process of Darwinian evolution within tissues1,4,5,6. Mutation, drift and selection in the large cell populations making up our tissues can result in the emergence of a clone that has acquired multiple genetic and epigenetic ‘driver’ alterations that disrupt tissue homeostasis and promote uncontrolled proliferation7,8,9,10. Although large-scale sequencing efforts over the last 20 years have provided comprehensive catalogues of the driver genes responsible for cancer development11,12,13, a complete quantitative understanding of the evolutionary dynamics governing how these drivers arise, expand and compete is lacking. Why are cancer driver mutations widespread across many healthy human tissues2,14,15,16,17, yet cancers of many of these tissues are comparatively rare? Why in some people do initial clonal expansions progress to lethal cancers whereas in others they remain benign? What are the relative roles of chance and determinism in the evolution of cancer? Answers to these questions could guide more rational approaches to early cancer detection18, risk prediction19,20,21,22,23 and personalized intervention24,25.

Theories of oncogenesis on the basis of somatic evolution have existed since the 1950s and were used to explain the nonlinear increases in cancer incidence with age26. These multi-stage models highlighted important roles for mutation26,27, selection28,29 and stem-cell population sizes30. However, these models have proven difficult to falsify with age-incidence data alone. The dynamics of molecular evolution, read-out using deep sequencing of serial samples, provide a more direct measure of the evolutionary dynamics and have transformed our understanding of microbial evolution31,32,33,34,35. Applying similar approaches to cancer development, however, has proven challenging as serial samples of pre-cancerous tissue from asymptomatic individuals are difficult to obtain. Even when these tissues are available, they typically provide only a static snapshot of the somatic diversity present. To better understand the dynamics of pre-cancerous evolution requires serial samples collected with high temporal resolution.

The haematopoietic system provides a unique opportunity to understand and quantify pre-cancerous evolution because serial blood samples in asymptomatic individuals can be collected antecedent to cancer development. Healthy blood displays ubiquitous and pronounced age-related changes driven by positive selection for genetic alterations that are recurrently mutated in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) (for example, DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1)19,20,21,22,23,36,37. This phenomenon, termed clonal haematopoiesis, increases the risk of future blood malignancies such as AML19,20,21,22,23. Although some aspects of clonal haematopoiesis evolution have begun to be understood quantitatively38,39,40,41,42,43, our understanding of how these age-related changes evolve into AML is incomplete. We reasoned that serial blood samples collected regularly over decade-long timescales in people who subsequently develop AML could be used to better understand the evolutionary origins of AML. By leveraging developments in error-correctable sequencing44,45 and insights from evolutionary theory32,46,47, we sought to characterize when in life the key driving events of AML occur and to gain insights into the rules governing their establishment, growth and competition.

The United Kingdom Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS) study enrolled 202,638 cancer-free post-menopausal women, aged 50–74 years, between 2001 and 2005, of whom 50,640 were randomized into a ‘multimodal arm’ involving annual blood serum samples for up to 11 years (refs. 3,48). We identified all the women who subsequently developed AML during more than 12 years of follow-up, of whom 47 had sufficient blood sample available from at least two timepoints before AML diagnosis. These 47 women were diagnosed with AML at a median age of 72 years (range 53–83 years) and had up to 10 serial blood samples (median 5) available before diagnosis (Fig. 1a, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Note 1). We obtained 249 pre-AML blood serum samples from these 47 women, as well as 249 timepoint-matched samples from 47 age-matched controls who remained cancer free. One control was subsequently excluded owing to development of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). To precisely track the evolutionary dynamics in these longitudinal samples, we designed a highly sensitive sequencing strategy called TETRIS-seq. This approach incorporates duplex error-corrected sequencing44 of a panel that comprehensively covers clonal haematopoiesis- and AML-associated genomic alterations, including gene mutations, chromosomal rearrangements and mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs), in combination with a custom in silico de-noising algorithm (Fig. 1b, Methods and Supplementary Note 2). Using TETRIS-seq we reliably achieved a duplex consensus depth of greater than 1,500×, enabling robust detection of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and indels at variant allele frequencies (VAFs) ≥0.1% (Supplementary Note 2f). Using the longitudinal nature of our samples, we phased single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) on sections of chromosomes affected by mCAs, enabling detection of chromosomal gains, losses and copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH) events ≥5 Mb down to approximately 1% cell fraction (Supplementary Note 2k,l).

a, Longitudinal blood samples collected annually from 47 future AML cases and 46 age-matched controls from the UKCTOCS cohort, up to ten samples per individual (one per timepoint). No technical replicates were performed. b, TETRIS-seq workflow for deep duplex targeted sequencing of AML-associated genetic alterations combined with an in silico de-noising algorithm. c, Cell fraction trajectories of all variants detected at more than one timepoint in the pre-AML cases (above; n = 132 variants) and controls (below; n = 59 variants), coloured by mutation gene class (see key). Characteristic dynamic behaviours are labelled and highlighted. Histograms (right) show the distribution of cell fraction measurements across all sampled timepoints (that is, one count per variant per timepoint).

Applying TETRIS-seq revealed strikingly different somatic evolutionary dynamics between the pre-AML cases and the controls (Fig. 1c). In controls, we detected clonal haematopoiesis in 72% (33 of 46) of people, consistent with previous studies37,39. Variants observed in controls were typically at cell fractions less than 20% and trajectories seemed relatively stable over time (Fig. 1c). These variants were mostly in well-known clonal haematopoiesis driver genes, including DNMT3A and TET2 (Extended Data Fig. 2). In pre-AML cases, we detected clonal haematopoiesis in 89% (42 of 47) of people. Compared with controls, variants observed in pre-AML cases were substantially more abundant and exhibited large cell fraction changes over the sampling period (Fig. 1c). These variants occurred in a broader range of AML-associated genes, including spliceosome, cell signalling and tumour suppressor genes (Extended Data Fig. 2).

The cell fraction trajectories observed in pre-AML samples exhibit a broad range of qualitative behaviours, which are distinct from the controls (highlighted trajectories, Fig. 1c). We observed many examples of classic selective sweeps whereby a single variant expanded to dominate the blood. Most of these somatic sweeps had already reached fixation before the sampling period (‘completed sweeps’). We did not detect any selective or completed sweeps in the controls. We also observed examples of clonal expansions whose growth stalled, reversed or experienced multiple reversals in fortune (Fig. 1c) suggestive of frequent and strong clonal interference between parallel lineages within the same individual. These behaviours were almost exclusively observed in the pre-AML cases. Clones expanding at low cell fraction were a common feature of both pre-AML cases and controls, but were more common in pre-AML cases (histograms, Fig. 1c) and seemed to expand at faster rates pre-AML.

The highly quantitative time-series data generated by TETRIS-seq enabled us to unambiguously infer the order of driver mutation acquisition and patterns of co-occurrence in many of the 47 pre-AML cases (Fig. 2, Supplementary Note 3, ‘Inferring clonal architecture’ in the Methods and Supplementary Table 8). In 55% (26 of 47) of pre-AML cases, we observed ‘linear evolution’, characterized by the sequential acquisition and expansion of driver mutations along a single dominant ‘trunk’, with minimal evidence of side-branching (Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Fig. 40). Within this class, however, there was substantial variation in the clonal composition of the blood in the decade before diagnosis. In 23% (11 of 47) of cases, we observed clear evidence of clonal interference, characterized by the acquisition and expansion of multiple driver clones on parallel evolutionary branches, which grew to high cell fractions (more than 10%) and interfered with each other’s growth, causing complex evolutionary trajectories (Fig. 2e–h and Supplementary Fig. 41). There was substantial variation in the dynamics observed within this class too, with examples of competition between quadruple-mutant clones (Fig. 2e), triple-mutant clones (Fig. 2h) and double-mutant clones (Fig. 2g). In both the linear and clonal interference patterns, most of the blood already derived from clones harbouring at least one pathogenic mutation in the decade pre-AML diagnosis. The remaining 21% (10 of 47) of cases are characterized by ‘late evolution’, for which the pre-leukaemic clone was detectable only 1–2 years pre-AML, if at all (Fig. 2i,j and Supplementary Fig. 42). This suggests that in some cases AML may evolve through the acquisition of uncommon driver mutations not covered by our targeted sequencing panel, that the pre-leukaemic evolution may play out while clones are below our detection limit or that the acquisition of the key drivers in these cases occurs without a long pre-leukaemic phase.

Muller plots showing inferred clonal dynamics in ten pre-AML cases, demonstrating ‘linear evolution’, ‘clonal interference’ or ‘late evolution’. Each panel is one pre-AML case. In each plot the vertical extent of a band is the fraction of cells belonging to that clone, with nested bands showing daughter clones arising within their parent, across age (x axis). Colour denotes the number of observed driver mutations in each clone (see legend); dark grey denotes the wild-type (non-driver) cell fraction. White vertical dashed lines indicate timing of UKCTOCS blood samples. Thick grey vertical dashed lines indicate time of AML diagnosis. The timing of any diagnosis of MDS, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML) or myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN), or pre-AML chemotherapy exposure, is indicated by labelled grey arrows (see Supplementary Table 10 for more details). a, Linear evolution: a double-mutant clone sweeps through the blood in the ~5 years before diagnosis. b, Linear evolution: a large single-mutant clone acquires further drivers in the final years before diagnosis. c, Linear evolution: a quadruple-mutant clone expands to dominate the blood. d, Linear evolution: the founding clone has already swept through the blood before sampling began, with a triple-mutant subclone expanding before diagnosis. e, Clonal interference between quadruple-mutant clones. f, Clonal interference between triple-mutant clones. g, Clonal interference between double-mutant clones. h, Clonal interference between triple-mutant clones. i, Late evolution: a putative pre-leukaemic clone first detected in the final year before diagnosis. j, Late evolution: a germline DDX41 carrier, with a small somatic DDX41/SRSF2-mutant clone detected only at the final sample. MF, myelofibrosis.

We reasoned that the high sensitivity and temporal resolution of our data could be used to gain a quantitative understanding of how driver mutations expand and compete in the decades preceding AML diagnosis (Fig. 3). We developed a mathematical framework for predicting how clones expand and compete through time inspired by models of microbial evolution32,46. In this framework the dynamics of a given clone are determined by its occurrence time, fitness effect and the simplest interaction term: an increasing ‘mean fitness’ of all other clones in the population that ensures the population frequencies of all clones sum to 1. The dynamics of a specific variant are determined by summing the frequency of the original parental clone (that is, the first clone to acquire the variant) and all daughter clones that inherited the variant (Fig. 3a–c).

a–c, Schematics demonstrating how clonal composition (left, phylogenetic trees) and the fitness and occurrence time of each clone (top plot) interact via the population mean fitness (black line, top plot) to produce different variant frequency trajectories (bottom plot). Annotations (for example, \(\bar{x}\) > s1) mark where the population mean fitness overtakes a clone’s fitness, driving the reversals seen in the trajectory. a, A single clone expands exponentially, slowing as the mean fitness rises and it sweeps to fixation. b, Competition between two independent clones: the less fit clone declines once its fitness is overtaken by the mean fitness. c, Competition within and between branches produces multiple reversals of fortune. d–g, Measured cell fractions (data points) compared with variant frequency trajectories (coloured lines) predicted from maximum likelihood estimates of each clone’s fitness and occurrence time, during UKCTOCS blood sampling (left plots) and since birth (right plots). Uncertainties (95% optimizer range and standard deviation) are provided in Supplementary Table 9. Grey shading indicates the UKCTOCS sampling window. Grey and thick black vertical dashed lines indicate blood samples and AML diagnosis, respectively. Labelled grey arrows indicate any other haematological malignancy, pre-AML cancer diagnosis or pre-AML chemotherapy exposure (Supplementary Table 10). Phylogenetic trees (right) show each clone’s inferred occurrence time (number in circles, years), fitness effect (% per year) and number of driver mutations (colour; see key). d, Linear evolution: a TET2-mutant clone acquired at ~39 years expands slowly until two further drivers are acquired 3 years before diagnosis. e, Linear evolution: an SRSF2/IDH2 double-mutant clone sweeps the blood, while low-frequency CHEK2 and IDH1 variants decline. f, Clonal interference on the background of a triple-mutant clone that had already swept the blood, resolved by an inferred missing driver (dashed line). g, Clonal interference with two inferred missing drivers (dashed lines).

After surviving an initial stochastic drift phase, a single clone carrying a driver mutation expands exponentially at a rate determined by its fitness (where ‘fitness’ is the growth rate relative to wild-type haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) assuming a constant effective population size). This clonal expansion causes the population mean fitness (\(\bar{x}\)) to increase, eventually causing the clonal expansion to slow down as it sweeps to fixation (Fig. 3a). Competition between two independent clones with different fitnesses can lead to the variant frequency trajectory of the less fit clone decreasing once its fitness is overtaken by the population mean fitness (Fig. 3b). Competition between clones within a branch and between branches can drive more complex variant frequency dynamics involving multiple reversals of fortune due to clones jumping ahead of, or falling behind, the population mean fitness (Fig. 3c). Using this framework, we developed a maximum likelihood approach (Methods) to infer fitness and occurrence time estimates for each clone and compare the predicted variant frequency trajectories (lines) with the measured trajectories (data points) in pre-AML cases (Fig. 3d–g, Extended Data Figs. 3–9 and Supplementary Fig. 47) and controls (Supplementary Figs. 48–55).

We observe a remarkably close agreement between the variant frequency trajectories predicted by this simple framework and the observed data. We first consider a case of linear evolution with no evidence of clonal competition (C92_005, Fig. 3d). Here we infer that a TET2 variant was acquired at around 39 years of age and expanded exponentially with a doubling time of about 2.4 years (fitness of 30% per year). Approximately 30 years later (at age approximately 67) this lineage acquires two further driver mutations that cause rapid clonal expansion, with a doubling time of about 8 weeks (fitness of ≥474% per year). Diagnosis occurs 3 years later at 70 years of age. Case C92_007 also exhibits a predominantly linear pattern of evolution (Fig. 3e). Here we infer that the first pre-leukaemic clone (SRSF2 p.P95L) is acquired at approximately 47 years of age and expands with a doubling time of about 2.5 years (fitness of 30% per year). Approximately 20 years later (at age around 67), this lineage acquires an IDH2 p.R140Q mutation, which creates a double-mutant clone that expands rapidly, with a doubling time of around 7 months (fitness effect of 115% per year). This double-mutant clone sweeps the blood when the person is in their late 70s and they are diagnosed with AML at age 80, 13 years after acquisition of the IDH2 mutation. The sweep of the double-mutant clone harbouring SRSF2 and IDH2 variants causes two low-frequency variants (in CHEK2 and IDH1) to be outcompeted, highlighting that high-frequency clones provide important information about the behaviour of low-frequency clones and vice versa.

We next considered cases with clear evidence of clonal interference (Fig. 3f,g). In C92_022 there has already been a full sweep of the blood by a clone harbouring three driver mutations (SRSF2 p.P95H and bi-allelic loss of TET2) by the time of the first sample, 8 years before diagnosis (Fig. 3f). On the background of this triple-mutant clone there is rapid evolution involving the acquisition of multiple further driver events. First, two independent clones caused by the acquisition of JAK2 V617F and MPL W515L arise at age approximately 55 and expand with doubling times of 4.3 and 6.7 months, respectively (fitness effects of about 195% and about 124% per year). These are soon outcompeted by a substantially fitter clone carrying 19p CN-LOH that is acquired at around 59 years of age and expands with a doubling time of just 2.4 months (fitness effect of about 345% per year). Remarkably, however, this lineage does not sweep. Instead, the JAK2 V617F lineage acquires two further events: a 9p CN-LOH and a subsequent event of unknown origin (‘missing driver’) that grows with a doubling time of about 1 month and sweeps the entire blood in under 2 years. Without invoking a highly fit missing driver (dashed trajectory, Fig. 3f), the variant frequencies measured at age 65 would be inconsistent with the behaviour of the observed clones. Thus, the internal consistency between the variant frequency trajectories can be used to detect events missed by our sequencing panel (Methods). C92_012 (Fig. 3g) highlights another example of clonal interference in which the observed VAF trajectories suggest the presence of two missing drivers. Despite these driver events being missed, the dynamics of the other observed driver events enable us to estimate their occurrence times and fitness effects.

Overall, these findings demonstrate that, once established in the HSC pool, the dynamics of pre-leukaemic clones are surprisingly predictable. Although we cannot exclude extrinsic effects altering some clones, one does not need to invoke more complex scenarios to explain the data: one can achieve remarkably close fits to variant trajectories by assuming clones have an intrinsic fitness and compete globally for one resource with minimal spatial structure.

Applying our framework to all pre-AML cases enabled us to estimate the fitness and occurrence time of many of the key events driving AML development in these 47 cases (Fig. 4) and 46 controls (Supplementary Figs. 48–56). In approximately 80% of pre-AML cases, our data suggest that the acquisition of the key driver events plays out over decades. In two-thirds of individuals who develop AML, the first driver mutation has already been acquired by age 20 (Fig. 4b). On average, these first driver events occur more than 50 years before AML diagnosis, but expand with relatively modest fitness advantages of around 10% to 30% per year (doubling times of about 2–7 years, Fig. 4c). A third of individuals have acquired their second driver mutation by age 50 (Fig. 4b). On average, these second ‘hits’ occur around 30 years before AML diagnosis and confer a substantially larger fitness advantage to cells, causing them to expand at rates of between about 20% and 100% per year (doubling times of about 1–3 years, Fig. 4c). Remarkably, this pattern continues as the pre-AML clone acquires further driver mutations. Clones with three driver mutations grow with fitness advantages of between around 50% and 200% per year, and quadruple-mutants range from around 100% to 1,000% per year, doubling in weeks to months (Fig. 4c). This remarkable increase in fitness with the number of driver mutations acquired is close to geometric: each driver mutation acquired confers a 2–3-fold increase in the growth rate. This finding strongly suggests that pre-leukaemic mutations combine synergistically.

The quantitative picture of the evolutionary dynamics afforded by our data highlights several important features. First, transformation usually involves the acquisition of multiple driver mutations in the same clone (range, 2–6), with considerable inter-patient variation in when these driver events are acquired. Second, pre-leukaemic clones are subject to strong positive selection, with fitness advantages that vary by two orders of magnitude: ranging from 10% per year for the least fit single-mutant clones to 1,000% per year for the fittest quadruple-mutant clones. Third, the variant frequency trajectories exhibit diverse qualitative behaviours, suggesting strong clonal competition in some cases (for example, C92_012 and C92_022) but a complete absence of competition in other cases (for example, C92_005 and C92_007).

We hypothesized that many of these features may be emergent properties of a stochastic evolutionary model governed by a simple set of rules. To test this, we developed a model of the clonal dynamics inspired by previous models of microbial evolution32,46,47, which we modified to incorporate key experimental observations (Methods). In this model, blood is maintained by a population of N cycling HSCs that divide symmetrically every \(\tau \) years (Fig. 5a). HSCs acquire driver mutations at a rate of U per year. Driver mutations vary in the fitness effects they confer to HSCs. A driver mutation arising in a wild-type HSC, creating a single-mutant clone, confers fitness advantages drawn from a distribution with a median and range controlled by a single parameter, s ≈ 16% per year (Methods). A driver mutation arising in a single-mutant clone confers a median fitness effect that is r = 2.5-fold larger (s ≈ 40% per year), creating a double-mutant clone. Triple-mutant and quadruple-mutant clones follow the same geometric pattern (with median fitness effects of s ≈ 100% and s ≈ 250% per year, respectively). In this framework, transformation to frank AML is defined by the acquisition of four driver mutations within the same clone that reaches greater than 50% of the cell fraction before the age of 85. Using established estimates for \(N\tau \)  = 105 (refs. 38,39,41), U ≈ 10−5 per year (ref. 40) and s ≈ 16% per year for single-mutant fitness effects39,42,43, we simulated the clonal dynamics in 200,200 simulations and considered the evolutionary dynamics observed in the decades preceding the around 900 virtual incidental AMLs (Fig. 5b–d).
