a, Developmental rate of embryos injected with H2B-mCherry mRNA (20 ng/µl) for live imaging assays. Left panel, representative images of embryos captured at the indicated time points (hpi). Two independent experiments with similar results (a). Tiled images from a large-field scan. b, 3D rendered images of mid 2-cell nuclei, related to Fig. 1b (additional examples from one experiment). The images labelled “paired” are from two blastomeres in a single embryo. c, Confocal 2D timelapse images of nuclei during the 1-cell, 2-cell and 4-cell stages. Representative from three independent experiments. The corresponding movies are provided in Supplementary Videos 1−3. The bright circular spots are nucleolus precursor bodies. d, Representative line profiles of local nuclear deformation, calculated as in inset. Negative signs indicate concave nuclear deformation. e, Time-dependent change in nuclear size, as measured by the mean nuclear radius R (mean ± s.d., n = 6 embryos). f, Time-dependent change in nuclear shape (traced outlines are overlaid). g, Representative confocal images of nuclei visualized using mCherry-NLS (red) and the traced outlines from two independent experiments. Statistical test, chi-square test (a). n, numbers of embryos analysed. Traces are representative from three independent experiments with similar results (d, f). Scale bars, 100 µm (a); 10 μm (b, c, g).

a–c, Influence of cytoplasmic viscosity. A viscous drag can oppose nuclear movement and affect the measurement; the effect may be larger at faster nuclear movement (a). The speed of nanocapillary movement among the developmental stages (b). The stage-dependent difference in nuclear deformability at varying nanocapillary speed (c). Coloured lines are linear regression slopes: 0.02, −0.01, 0.08, 0.06, and 0.01 (min) for the 1-cell, early 2-cell, mid 2-cell, late 2-cell and 4-cell stages, respectively. The values in b are 0.26 ± 0.19 µm/sec (1-cell), 0.24 ± 0.05 µm/sec (early 2-cell), 0.28 ± 0.18 µm/sec (mid 2-cell), 0.28 ± 0.12 µm/sec (late 2-cell) and 0.29 ± 0.18 µm/sec (4-cell) (n = 27, 17, 18, 20 and 25 embryos, respectively). d–f, Influence of cytoplasmic elasticity. An elastic restoring force can oppose nuclear movement and affect the measurement (d). The movements of nuclei before and after micromanipulation from their original location in embryos (D1 and D2 in d, respectively) (e). The stage-dependent difference in nuclear deformability at varying nuclear travel distance (f). Coloured lines are linear regression slopes: 0.22, 0.18, 0.26, 0.19, and 0.22 for the 1-cell, early 2-cell, mid 2-cell, late 2-cell and 4-cell stages, respectively (the identical numbers of embryos per condition as in a–c). g, h, Nuclear stiffness measured using different imaging probes (g) and label-free differential interference contrast (DIC) imaging (h). H2B-mCherry: n = 18, 13, 12, 13 and 13 embryos (from Fig. 1j,k), emerin-EGFP: n = 12, 6, 14, 6 and 9 embryos; label-free DIC imaging: n = 12, 6 and 7 embryos, from the 1-cell to 4-cell stages, respectively. i, Nuclear stiffness variation in individual embryos. The lines connecting the plots indicate paired data from each (pro)nucleus in the same embryos (8 and 16 pairs for 1-cell and 2-cell, respectively). j, Influence of nanocapillary pressure levels on the measured nuclear stiffness (n = 13 and 45 embryos for 2.1 × 101 kPa and 1.2 × 101 kPa among the population that reached the blastocyst stage at 96 hpi, respectively). k, Influence of nanocapillary pressure levels on the frequency of development. Data from three to four independent experiments per condition (black circles). Total numbers of embryos: n = 55, 64, 75 embryos, from left to right columns. Bars are s.d. H2B-mcherry (20 ng/µl mRNA) was used as nuclear marker (i–k). l–n, Alternative mechanical measurement using aspiration force. Nuclear surface was aspirated using an incremental suction pressure (6 × 103 Pa/min) applied to a capillary (l). Confocal images (m, H2B-mCherry) were used to determine the pressure level at which the nucleus began to be aspirated (>1 µm) (n). The values are 11.5 ± 5.5 kPa (1-cell), 3.8 ± 1.4 kPa (2-cell) and 10.4 ± 2.5 kPa (4-cell) (n = 12, 14 and 12 embryos, respectively). Statistical tests, Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test (b, e, h, n) (comparison was performed independently for D1 and D2 in e); Mann–Whitney U test (two-sided) (g, j); Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-sided) (i); one-way ANOVA followed by Turkey’s multiple comparison test (k). The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means. Scale bars, 10 μm.

a, Snapshots (overlay of bright-field and H2B-EGFP) of 2-cell nuclei in IVF (left panels) and SCNT (right panels) embryos subjected to nanocapillary-based mechanical analysis, associated with data in Fig. 2. Representative from three independent experiments. b, Effect of nuclear imaging marker on nuclear stiffness measurement examining IVF embryos (H2B-mCherry: n = 53 embryos, H2B-EGFP: n = 28 embryos; from Fig. 2b). c, Expression levels of nuclear imaging marker in IVF embryos that reached the blastocyst stage versus ones that exhibited impaired development (pooled from H2B-mCherry and H2B-EGFP samples). Blue-coloured plots are samples that showed stiff 2-cell nuclei, defined as more than twice the mean in normally developed embryos. The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means. d, Representative images and the frequency of preimplantation development for SCNT embryos with and without nanocapillary-based measurement (n = 46 and 52 embryos, respectively) from three independent experiments. e, Tables show the developmental impairment of each embryo and the corresponding nuclear stiffness measured at the 2-cell stage. Statistical test, Mann–Whitney U test (two-sided) (b, c). Scale bars, 10 µm (a); 50 μm (d).

Lysates of 2-cell embryos (32 hpi; 60 embryos per sample) injected with EGFP-sfLB1 mRNA (right lane) were blotted along with control (left lane). j, Immunoblotting of endogenous lamin B1 in 2-cell embryos perturbed via sfLB1 (28 hpi; 25 embryos per sample, middle lane). a–e, Quantitative assessment of 6× expansion microscopy. a, The extent of sample expansion. The average radii of the nuclei before and after expansion were compared (pre-ExM; 9.0 ± 0.6 µm, ExM; 53.6 ± 3.8 µm, n = 12 embryos each). b–e, Quantification of nuclear shape parameters. The aspect ratio (b), roundness (c), local deformation (d) and solidity (e) of 2-cell nuclei with and without expansion were compared. f, Representative ExM images of mid 2-cell nuclei (24 hpi) in control embryos (top panels, n = 7 embryos) and those overexpressing lamin B1 mutants (middle and bottom panels, n = 7 and 6 embryos, for flLB1(5 A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A), respectively). Linescans were generated along the nuclear periphery. g, h, Normalized coefficient of variance of peripheral lamin B1 (g) and DNA (h) signals for the control and the mutants from linescans as in f. i, Intensity profiles of DNA and lamin B1 signals across the 2-cell nuclear periphery (n = 12 embryos; non-injection). Representative from n = 6 embryos, two independent experiments. k, Correlations between DNA signal intensity and nuclear deformation in control embryos and those perturbed via lamin B1 mutants. l, The site occupancy of strong DNA signals in concave versus convex regions of the nuclear envelope. m, Correlations between lamin B1 signal and nuclear deformation. n = 12, 8 and 15 embryos for control, flLB1(5 A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A), respectively (k–m). a, Schematic of the RNA-seq analysis. b, Scatter plots and Pearson correlation coefficients comparing gene expression profiles among Non, flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) (three biological replicates each). c, Hierarchical clustering dendrogram generated from the gene expression profiles of individual samples (Pearson correlation). d, PCA of the gene expression profiles. e, MA plots showing the DEGs between Non vs flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC (three biological replicates each). f–n, RNA-seq analysis data for sfLB1. a, Immunostaining of 2-cell embryos prepared under various permeabilization conditions prior to fixation. The conventional Cut & Tag method includes the cell permeabilization step for Tn5 and antibodies to access the intracellular environment. However, the recommended duration of Triton X-100 exposure (more than 5 min) altered DNA localization of 2-cell embryos. We therefore titrated the Triton X-100 exposure duration and found that 30 s of Triton X-100 treatment was sufficient for the lamin B1 antibody to bind to its antigen while retaining normal DNA localization. b, A schematic diagram of the Cut&Tag analysis process for embryos with or without inhibition of lamin B1 clearance. c, Pearson correlation coefficient of mapped H3K4me3 signals among different samples. Two biological replicates, annotated as numbers in each sample label. d, A hypergeometric test was performed to compare the distribution of H3K4me3 peaks among our Cut&Tag samples and the previously published H3K4me3 ChIP-seq dataset14,30. P values are shown for each comparison. e, Track images of Cut&Tag and the published ChIP-seq reads around the Kdm5b gene. Locations of major ZGA genes and downregulated genes in sfLB embryos are indicated at the bottom. f, g, H3K4me3 signal intensities around downregulated genes in sfLB1 embryos (f) and around lamina-associated domains40 (g) for sfLB and noninjected embryos. An accumulation of H3K4me3 around downregulated genes in the sfLB1-expressing embryos (f).

Representative confocal time-lapse images of H2B-mcherry in embryos (representative from data in h) expressing either the wild-type tether (WT) or its mutant derivatives (LaG165A or titinW34E) during the first cleavage (g). The timings of nuclear envelope break-down (NEBD) and the completion of mitosis were analysed based on nuclear/chromosome signals, with no statistical significance for the 2-cell entry (p > 0.05 by the chi-square test) (h). The signals were calculated as an integrated intensity in each embryo and normalized to the mean value of the wild-type control (n = 13, 9 and 9 embryos from left to right). k, Developmental rate analysed for embryos expressing the wild-type tether or its mutant derivatives (LaG165A and titinW34E) along with the anchor. n, numbers of embryos analysed. #2007. Scotland face a mountainous task - but rewards are worth the climb

To emphasis the scale of what faces Scotland at the Sitterstadion in St Gallen on Monday night, the national team is looking to repeat a feat only carried out by Germany and Spain over the past two years.

Switzerland don’t lose often on home soil under Murat Yakin. The Germans and the world champions have prevailed in the Alps that period. In short, it takes a very good performance to leave with the full loot. And for Scotland to stand a chance in achieving their objective and finishing second in Nations League Group B1, they need to win.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Even then, it might not be enough. Sitting third on seven points going into Monday’s final round of matches, Scotland trail second-placed Slovenia by a point. Should the Slovenians defeat bottom-of-the-table North Macedonia in Skopje, the Scots could win 5-0 and it wouldn’t change the standings.

A draw won’t help either, as Slovenia have a better head-to-head record over Scotland by virtue of their 2-1 win at Hampden last month.

Ending up second is important. It would move Scotland into a play-off spot and a chance of promotion to Nations League A. It would also ensure a second seeding for the Euro 2028 qualification draw next month. Scotland are a host nation for the tournament, and getting in through the back door of a reserved place for non-qualifiers would be embarrassing - although not as humiliating as not being there at all.

The odds of toppling Slovenia, however, are stacked against Scotland. It requires two surprise results. North Macedonia have been meek throughout this campaign and have no points to show for their name, even if their display at Hampden on Friday showed glimmers of improvement in a 2-1 loss. The Scots need a favour in the Balkans.

Switzerland may give Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli some optimism. Yakin is planning to shuffle his pack after landing top spot with a game to spare. Some of the star Swiss names may be kept in reserve. Granit Xhaka, Manuel Akanji, Dan Ndoye and Johan Manzambi are definitely out.

Nevertheless, Yakin vowed that his team will still be strong,. “It has happened a few times already. But we will make sure we get good level of player onto the pitch.

“It’s good thing we have won the group already. It’s now an opportunity to make changes. It doesn’t make sense to wait for injuries players. We have enough opportunities and possibilities.

“We will rotate a but but we first have to make sure that we have a stable defence with experienced defenders. Of course, we will try to get as many players involved as possible. There are a lot of players who haven’t played at all, so they can play from the start.

“We want our boys to get a chance and look forward to it and show their best game. We will certainly make some changes in attack.”

It is of benefit to Scotland that they face an opponent with nothing on the line. Especially as there are areas of concern over how the team has fared so far under Pocognoli’s watch.

The game against Switzerland will be Pocognoli’s sixth in charge after two wins against North Macedonia, two defeats (Switzerland and Slovenia at home) and a draw in Ljubljana. The performance on Friday was far from convincing, but for Pocognoli to get his first win at Hampden should have lifted a bit of weight from the 39-year-old Belgian’s shoulders.

Pocognoli stuck with a back three and Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney coped pretty well with North Macedonia’s blunt attack. The visitors’ goal came from a set-piece and they didn’t look good enough to score in open play, even if they had attacking moments.

The worry for many Scotland fans is that better teams will punish Scotland when they either counter-attack or break through the press. Pocognoli’s insistence on playing a high line and asking his team to be proactive most of the time means that the defence does get exposed. And the top teams will take advantage.

Shorn of many defenders, it is likely Pocognoli will stick with the same back three. There is clamour for a back four, but the head coach will surely be reluctant to throw away all of his work thus far. His biggest conundrum is whether to keep winger Ben Gannon-Doak as his right wing-back or deploy the more rounded and defensively-savvy Aaron Hickey there.

On the other flank, a massive piece of history will be made. Captain Andy Robertson will win his 103rd cap and become Scotland’s most-capped male player of all time. It is an incredible achievement for the 32-year-old, who has been front and centre of Scotland’s recent renaissance and while he will try to shrug off the limelight, this night does belong to him.

Robertson will not want such a milestone tarnished by a defeat and neither will his team-mates. “It just takes time to click but it’s up to us as players now to show we can do what he wants,” said striker Che Adams of Pocognoli’s philosophy. “We have been together for a number of years now so we know each other’s game. You could see on Friday us starting to put the manager’s things in practice, we won a lot of balls high with our pressing.

“Coming off a transitional period like we have just now, it’s difficult to know where you are and what you want to do. But all the boys here want to play for our country and do Scotland proud.”

A win in Switzerland would do the nation proud. Depending on what happens 990 miles down the road in Skopje, it may or may not be enough to finish second in the group, but a positive display would give Scotland something to build upon next year when the Euro 2028 qualifiers start and give a sceptical public reasons for optimism.

#2006. I watched Scotland sneak past Wallabies and noted two big replacement plus Rangers stars in stands

Scotland got back on the winning trail with a 15-12 victory over Australia at Murrayfield.

After the disappointment of losing heavily to New Zealand eight days ago, head coach Gregor Townsend will have been pleased to see his team recover - although the triumph was far from swashbuckling.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Mark Atkinson was at Murrayfield to cover proceedings for The Scotsman and picks out some talking points from the match:

Winning was clearly the most important thing for Scotland, which is why with eight minutes to go, Finn Russell took the three points from a penalty rather than going for touch to push for a try.

It moved Scotland ten points clear and left Australia with too much to do, even with Max Jorgensen’s late try to keep the game very close.

However, Scotland’s inability to rack up the points is likely to harm them in the wider scale of the Nations Championship.

With one round of fixtures remaining before finals weekend, Scotland sit fourth in the standings on 15 points with a points difference of -8. After their historic win over New Zealand, fifth-placed Wales also have 15 points but with a points difference of -28. They face Australia next, which is winnable.

Scotland take on whipping boys Japan at Murrayfield on Saturday and need to win comprehensively with a bonus point to put pressure on third-placed Ireland and second-placed England, who are on 20 points and have points differences of +57 and +134 respectively.

Ireland take on South Africa and England face New Zealand, where a solitary bonus point will ensure either of them a top-three finish - and given England’s point difference, it would take something special to overhaul them. Scotland's best hope is probably a big Springbok win.

The chances are Scotland will finish fourth - which would mean a play-off against either Argentina or Australia.

Scotland did not play with much verve or pizzazz and were lamentably wasteful at the start of the second half when Billy Pollard was sent to the sin bin. Rather than adding to the scoreboard, they gave away two cheap penalties and lost their own lineout in a promising position.

Playmaker Russell failed to ignite the game and was patchy with some of his kicking, while the ball very rarely made it out to the wide players.

It wasn’t a game that got the pulses racing and Scotland will likely pay the price.

While both teams will rue not scoring a bucketload of points, there will be some satisfaction from the defensive effort given what happened the previous weekend.

Scotland shipped 43 points to the All Blacks and Australia were on the end of 45 points at Twickenham. It was evident that both sides were intent on keeping the door shut.

While imagination was at a premium, there were a lot of good tackles and discipline when pressure was on. Australia boss Les Kiss referenced it afterwards and Townsend will be pleased with the way his team held firm in difficult conditions for the majority of the final 20 minutes.

Darcy Graham’s tackle right at the end on Tom Wright ensured the win for Scotland and must be applauded for his work at the death.

Scotland had to turn to their bench before and after kick-off, and the replacements did themselves no harm.

Tom Jordan was a last-minute sub for captain Sione Tuipulotu, who failed a late fitness test due to a knee injury. The Bristol Bears man is a versatile fellow and while he’s more often than not been used at 10 or 15 for Scotland, he was asked to partner Huw Jones at centre.

This wasn’t a game for creativity, but Jordan did have some nice offloads and he defended well. If Tuipulotu doesn’t make next week against Japan, Jordan has probably kept himself ahead of Stafford McDowall.

In the pack, Scott Cummings pulled up on 25 minutes and the lock was replaced by his Glasgow Warriors club-mate Max Williamson, who made his presence felt with some big hits and powerful work at the breakdown.

Williamson has found himself behind Cummings and another Glasgow man in Gregor Brown, but this was a performance that will give Townsend food for thought for the rest of the year.

Blair Kinghorn used to be a nailed-on starter for Scotland, but his own form at Toulouse, niggling injuries and the emergence of Kyle Rowe at Glasgow Warriors has put his position in jeopardy.

Townsend gave Kinghorn the whole match at full-back and he served up a reminder of why he can make a difference in the Test arena.

He was secure under the high ball, ran with purpose and broke the line on several occasions. He also put in an excellent tackle on Jorgensen at a crucial point in the game.

Many feel Rowe was unfortunate not to feature against Australia, but Kinghorn has that little bit extra physicality and oomph that sets him apart.

We are also in the midst of an international break in football and that allowed a couple of Rangers players to take in this match.

Scotland striker Lawrence Shankland and Australia midfielder Cammy Devlin are both currently injured, so they were able to watch on in the Murrayfield stands without any commitments - and not far from their old stomping ground.

The ex-Hearts duo seemed to be enjoying the game and Shankland will no doubt have liked Scotland landing the bragging rights over the Wallabies.

#2005. Celtic treble winner promises to ‘lead change in football’ as he launches bid to overthrow Infantino

Former Celtic defender Ramon Vega has confirmed that he is launching a bid to replace Gianni Infantino as FIFA President at next year’s elections, saying that football must be “for the people, not those who control it.”

Vega, 55, spent a brief but memorable loan spell at Celtic in the second half of the 2000/01 campaign, scoring twice on his debut in a 6-0 win over Aberdeen. He also had spells at Tottenham Hotspur and Cagliari during his 13-year career, and earned 23 caps for Switzerland.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

During his six-month loan stint at Celtic Park, Vega quickly developed into a fan favourite as part of a Martin O'Neill side that lifted a domestic treble in 2001. However, his stay in Glasgow was brief, and he signed for Watford on a free transfer shortly afterwards, after the London club offered him the security of a longer contract at Vicarage Road.

Retiring two years later, he has forged a successful career in global finance and asset management, but Vega now believes the time is right to oust under-pressure President Infantino when the elections formally take place at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco next March.

The Swiss defender, who can speak six languages, has ran for the role three times previously, in 2015, 2019 and 2023, but maintains his belief that he can succeed in his bid to become the next FIFA President, stating that “football stands at a defining crossroads” and that “the decisions we make today will shape the future of our beautiful game for generations to come.”

Writing on his official X (formerly Twitter) account, he said on Sunday: “A credible FIFA begins with a credible election. UEFA provided Infantino with €500,000 in official campaign funding to support his global travel and logistics ahead of the February 2016 FIFA Extraordinary Congress. Europe played a decisive role in bringing the current leadership to FIFA therefore also has a huge responsibility to help bring about change.

“I call for open and transparent dialogue across the entire global football family. Major decisions affecting our game should never be imposed. They must follow genuine consultation, where every voice is heard and the broadest possible consensus is built before decisions are made. The solution is a credible candidate, a democratic election, a clear program capable of restoring trust, integrity, transparency and unity.

“I offer every member association a neutral, independent and credible democratic alternative, a candidate rooted in the game, who can bridge football and international finance &business, bring cultures together and lead FIFA with competence, integrity and independence. For me serving football is not about personal ambition. It's a responsibility, a duty and a matter of honour.”

To officially run for the Presidency, the former Celtic man must win the backing of five or more national federations before Wednesday’s [November 18] deadline. However, this could be possible, with Vega claiming he has backing across every continent, though he has yet to reveal who is endorsing him.

#2004. Rangers star saved by Man Utd man as team secure quarter-final place with stunning comeback

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin breathed a sigh of relief after seeing the penalty he conceded just minutes after his introduction to the pitch saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens during Belgium’s thumping 4-1 win over Italy in the Nations League on Sunday night.

Despite starting Belgium’s 2-1 win away over Turkiye on Thursday night, the Rangers star had to be content with a place on the bench against Italy as Mark van Bommel’s side looked to seal a place in the quarter-finals of the Nations League at the Stade Roi Baudouin.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Two points ahead of their visitors ahead of the Group A1 clash on nine points, the game got off to a disastrous start for the hosts when Italy went into an 11th-minute lead when Brentford defender Michael Kayode's cross to Pio Esposito to score 10th international goal in 15 appearances.

However, the lead was short-lived, and Belgium found themselves back on level terms just four minutes later when Brighton wing-back Maxim de Cuyper slammed home to restore parity in Brussels, before centre-back Nathan Ngoy rifled home from close range after a scramble in the box on 22 minutes.

Jeremy Doku then completed the turnaround when he added a third for Belgium just four minutes later, dancing through the Italian defence with stunning footwork before firing a low drive beyond his Manchester City teammate Gianluigi Donnarumma in the visitor’s goal. The strike put his side temporarily top of Group A1, with Turkiye holding France to a 0-0 draw at half-time.

With 10 minutes to spare, Diego Moreira made sure of the win when he neatly placed home his side’s fourth of the game after being teed up by Kevin De Bruyne. However, it was not enough to seal top spot in the group, with Belgium forced to be content with qualification to the Nations League quarter-finals via second place as France ran out 2-1 winners in Paris.

Despite the Group standings being all but confirmed, the action did not cease, with Italy awarded a last-minute penalty after VAR ruled that Raskin had handled Alphadjo Cisse’s shot in the area. The Rangers man had replaced Romeo Lavia just over 10 minutes earlier, but needn’t have worried, as goalkeeper Lammens pulled off an excellent save to deny Esposito a brace.

“If Donnarumma had not been in goal, then we would've scored six,” said new Belgium head coach van Bommel. “I'll be honest, I didn't expect this when we started two months ago, but even before that first match with Italy, I could tell this was a really intelligent group of players. That makes it a pleasure for a coach to work with them.

“These players can anticipate an opponent, are flexible, and can adapt to different situations. Today you saw that reflected. Not only was the idea right, individually many players stepped up too. And ultimately we managed to dominate an opponent like Italy for long periods. That is the most important thing to me."

Belgium will discover their Nations League quarter-final opponents on Friday, November 20, 2026, with the draw set to take place at 11am UK time in Nyon, Switzerland.

#2003. 'No point' - Former QPR and Charlton striker has say on Crawley Town strategy for next manager

That’s the view of former QPR and Charlton striker Conor Washington as he has his say on Crawley Town’s next managerial appointment.

Reds owners have yet to name a permanent successor for Colin Kazim-Richards, who was sacked on October 21 following a poor start to the season which has sees them rock bottom of League Two.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Kevin Blackwell has been in charge on an interim basis but Reds fans are eagerly anticipating who will be the next permanent boss as they look to climb the table.

But Washington, in his latest exclusive EFL column for BestBettingBonuses.co.uk, says there is a bigger picture at play.

“I think the bigger question for me is around the overall football strategy at the club,” he said. “With the structure they've got, they either need to decide on a clear way they want the club to play, recruit players who fit that and then appoint managers who can implement it, or they need to appoint a manager with a really clear playing style and back him with recruitment that suits what he's trying to do. Both approaches can work, but you can't really keep moving between the two.

"Otherwise you end up with players recruited for one manager being asked to play a completely different way under the next one.

“From what Colin Kazim-Richards said in the summer, there was clearly an attempt to recruit players specifically for his ideas, but now they're potentially looking for another manager just a few months later. That's where the problems can start.”

And he added that it’s a big job for whoever comes in. He said: “I think whoever comes in needs to be really clear about what they've inherited, what the players are actually capable of and how they can get the best out of them.

"There's no point appointing someone because you like their philosophy if the squad isn't equipped to carry it out, particularly when you're fighting to stay in the league.”

Reds face Fleetwood Town at home on Saturday following their international break.

#2002. There's still a place in the modern game for managers like Kevin Blackwell, says former Hearts and Rotherham United striker

Kevin Blackwell has been in charge of Crawley Town on an interim basis since the end of October following the sacking on Colin Kazim-Richards after a terrible start to the season for the Reds.

The 67-year-old has a vast amount of managerial experience including jobs at Leeds United and Sheffield United and, despite an embarrassing exit in the FA Cup to seventh tier Wimborne Town, has had a good start to his Reds stint with four points in two league games.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

And Washington, in his latest exclusive EFL column for BestBettingBonuses.co.uk, is happy to see Blackwell involved.

“I think it's great to see genuine football people like Kevin still involved in the game,” he said. “Football feels very modern and young at the minute, and sometimes it seems like coaches are inventing new vocabulary every other week to describe things we've been doing for decades!

“The reality is that so much of what we're seeing tactically has been done before in some way, shape or form. Of course the game evolves and you have to adapt with it, but the fundamental aim of football hasn't changed.”

And he added that experience can be seen as detrimental sometimes when it comes to older managers. He said: “So much of management is still about understanding people, building relationships and helping players through difficult situations. I think we're sometimes too quick to dismiss experienced managers or label them as dinosaurs because they might talk about defending deep rather than playing in a low block.

" Ultimately, they're describing the same thing, and just because someone doesn't use the latest terminology doesn't mean they don't understand the game.”

But Washington said experience is what Reds need right now. “In Crawley's situation, I think having someone who's experienced difficult periods before and isn't afraid to be demanding could be exactly what the players need,” he said.

"That doesn't necessarily mean being abrasive for the sake of it, but sometimes players need clarity, honesty and someone who's prepared to make difficult decisions.”

But should Blackwell be considered for the job permanently? Washington said: “I think that should come down to the impact he has on the players and the results he gets, rather than any preconceived ideas about his style or personality.

"There's absolutely still a place in the modern game for managers like Kevin, and I think it would be a shame if we lost sight of that.”

#2001. Rangers hitman makes impact off the bench but late goal sees team sink to record breaking low

Naderi, who opted to represent Czechia last month despite also being eligible to represent Germany and Bulgaria, made his international debut as a second-half substitute in a 3-1 defeat to world champions Spain in October before making his full debut against England at Wembley a few days later.

However, they started the game in the worst possible fashion, with veteran winger Ivan Perisic putting the home side ahead after just 87 seconds via a clinical left-footed strike from the edge of the penalty area.

Searching for a quickfire second, Croatia piled on the pressure following their early opener, but Czechia stood firm until half-time. Looking to restore parity, Czechia began to get back into the game after the restart, with Antonin Kinsky, Idris Hopi and Adam Hlozek all attempting to get past Barcelona stopper Dominik Livakovic in the home side’s net. His initial effort was blocked, but Hlozek reacted quickest to rifle home a left-footed finish to level the level. However, just as it appeared that Naderi’s had helped his side steal a late point, Croatia restored their lead three minutes later through substitute Lovro Majer.

Taking a pass from Brighton centre-back Luka Vuskovic in the away side’s area, he drilled a low drive into the net to condemn Czechia to a seventh consecutive defeat and the worst losing streak in their history.

Beginning in the group stages of this summer’s World Cup in North America, Czechia’s slide began with a 3-0 defeat to Mexico and has carried straight through into a brutal Nations League campaign against Spain, England, and Croatia.

#2000. When is the Nations League quarter-finals draw? TV and streaming details, plus how to watch

The group stage of the Nations League is almost at a close, with the final fixtures taking place this week across Europe.

Set to begin in March, sides from League A will have their sights set on lifting the Nations League title, while League B, C and D nations fight it out for promotion and relegation.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Won by Portugal last year, they claimed a second title with a penalty shootout win over Spain after playing out a thrilling 2-2 draw with Spain in Munich, Germany. Winners of the inaugural tournament in 2019, they are now the most successful team in Nations League history, ahead of Spain and France, who have one win each.

Want to know when the draw for the Nations League quarter-final takes place, who has qualified and when the games will take place? Here’s everything you need to know:

Get our daily football newsletter by clicking here.

The draw for the Nations League quarter-finals will take place on Friday, 20 November. The draw begins at 11am UK time and will take place at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

As of November 15, the following teams have confirmed a place in the Nations League quarter-finals: France, Belgium, England, Portugal and Spain.

In total, eight teams qualify for the quarter-finals via League A. The four League A group winners are seeded and placed in Pot 1 of the draw, with the four League A group runners-up are placed in Pot 2 and unseeded. Each group winner is drawn against a runner-up from a different group. Teams from the same group cannot play each other in the quarter-finals.

Teams placed in Leagues B, C and D all compete for promotion and relegation, and are unable to qualify for the knockout stage of the competition.

The upcoming quarter-final ties will be played over two legs during the March 2027 international break. The seeded group winners will play the first leg away from home, with the second leg on home soil. First legs are scheduled to take place from 25–27 March 2027, and second legs follow from 28–30 March 2027.

The draw will not be broadcast in the UK and Ireland. However, they are several options to stream the draw live, which are detailed below.

If you want to stream the draw via your smart TV, laptop, tablet or mobile phone, the entire ceremony will be streamed for free via UEFA.tv and via the official UEFA YouTube channel.

#1998. Manchester United hit with new injury concern ahead of Mauricio Pochettino arrival

Manchester United have been hit with a fresh injury concern as Patrick Dorgu has withdrawn from international duty with Denmark.

The 22-year-old suffered a hamstring injury during Denmark’s 2-0 win over Wales in September and was out until he made his return in United’s 4-4 draw with Aston Villa last Sunday.

Dorgu had been called up to Denmark’s squad for their Nations League fixtures against Portugal and Norway.

But the versatile left-sider will not feature in either game for Denmark and has returned to United due to his injury.

Speaking on Friday, Denmark’s team doctor, Morten Boesen, said: ‘We have carried out a series of tests on Dorgu, and he has not performed well enough to be ready to play in the two matches.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘He needs further recovery time after his injury, so we are sending him home for additional rehabilitation.’

Meanwhile, Mauricio Pochettino was officially confirmed as United’s new head coach on Friday following the club’s decision to sack Michael Carrick.

Pochettino will take charge of the United States’ games against Haiti on November 14 and 17 before travelling to Manchester ahead of United’s next Premier League game away to Liverpool on November 22.

During a press conference on Friday, Pochettino was in tears as he was asked why he took the United job having signed a new four-year contract with the United States Soccer Federation in August.

‘It’s difficult to talk now. I’m a very emotional guy. It’s a very sad decision,’ Pochettino said.

‘But we are professionals and we are trying to make our dreams come true.

‘I never said I wanted to go back [to the Premier League] but they know there aren’t too many opportunities that happen in your career like Manchester United. When it arrives, it’s difficult to turn down.’

#1997. How Scotland can qualify for Nations League playoffs, and how third place finish affects Euro 2028 qualifiers

Scotland end their Nations League campaign with a clash against Switzerland on Monday, with their slim hopes of qualifying for the promotion playoffs still intact.

Placed in Group B1 alongside Slovenia, North Macedonia and the aforementioned Switzerland, new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli kept alive Scotland’s chances of claiming second spot in the group with a narrow 2-1 home win over North Macedonia on Friday, thanks to two goals from John McGinn.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Here’s what Scotland needs to happen to nab a promotion/relegation playoff spot, how to watch the draw and what a third-placed finish would mean for Pocognoli’s men.

First and foremost, Scotland MUST beat Switzerland to stand any chance of finishing in second place in the group. Should they achieve that, they will also have to hope Slovenia fail to beat North Macedonia. If Slovenia beat North Macedonia this evening, it is impossible for Scotland to finish in second place regardless of their result against Switzerland.

In the scenario that Scotland draw with Switzerland, and Slovenia lose to North Macedonia, both sides would be level on eight points. However, Slovenia would take second place following their 2-1 win at Hampden Park last month, with UEFA prioritizing head-to-head results between tied teams rather than overall goal difference. Currently in third place on seven points, they trail Slovenia in second place on eight points.

The draw for the Nations League playoffs will take place on Friday, 20 November. The draw begins at 11am UK time and will take place at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

You can stream the draw live via your smart TV, laptop, tablet or mobile phone, the entire ceremony will be streamed for free via UEFA.tv and the official UEFA YouTube channel.

If Scotland fail to beat Switzerland in their final Group B1 game, they will be guaranteed to finish in the third place and will remain in League B for the next edition of the tournament. North Macedonia are already guaranteed to finish fourth place will face a promotion/relegation playoff game with a second-placed League C team to remain in League B. Scotland are safe from relegation to League B.

Meanwhile, Switzerland have already won the group and have been promoted to League A. As detailed above, the second place team [currently Slovenia] will face a playoff against a third placed League A side.

A third placed finish will have a direct effect on Scotland’s Euro 2028 qualifying campaign, which begins in March 2027. The tournament, which takes place across the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland, will require all four co-hosts - England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland - to compete in the standard qualifying campaign. They are not given a bye.

Where teams finish in their Nations League groups will directly decide how they are seeded for Euro 2028 qualifying, with each nation seeded based on their final group position. If Scotland finish in third, then Pocognoli’s side would drop into pot three for the draw, which could result in them facing high-ranking opponents from Pot 1 and Pot 2.

The Euro 2028 qualifying draw sees teams separated into 12 groups of either four or five teams. Those who win their groups groups qualify automatically for the finals, alongside the eight highest ranked second place finishers. The four lowest ranked second place finishers enter the play-offs. Team who finish third or lower will not qualify.

The one caveat is that the host nations have two spots in the finals reserved if they fail to qualify. If more than two host teams do not qualify via the usual route, these two places will be allocated to the hosts placed highest in the European Qualifiers overall rankings. If only one or neither of the spots be used, the remaining places will be reallocated via the play-offs.

#1996. Thoughts of a lifelong fan: Fingers-crossed for a first home win and a night off for Kabby

I am just about getting over our exit from the FA Cup and the Jersey Mike’s Trophy, watching Exeter City go one up against CTFC (the other one), and in visiting OUR club’s website I was shocked to see we only have just over an hour to go before we play Rotherham away.

We don’t of course, because of international call ups for both sides. The three for Crawley being Dion Pereira, Stephen Duke-McKenna and Nick Michalski. Dion played for 60 minutes for Antigua and Barbuda in a 3-2 home defeat, whilst Nick was in goal for the England U20 side in  a 6-1 win against Czechia and Stephen was scoring a brace for Guyana in a six nil away victory over the Cayman Islands. I hope it’s not too long before he is scoring again for Crawley.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Going back to "us” playing at Rotherham, and with just 40 minutes to kick off, “I follow” will sell you an audio pass to the game if you want to listen, surely this rivals the notice board outside the Broadfield stadium in not showing the club in the best light. In the old days, and I know this makes me sound like everyone’s dad or Uncle Albert, Stan Markham would have the next match on the board at half time while people were still watching the game and we didn't have the internet, but I'm sure we wouldn’t have been advertising something that wasn’t going to take place.

Of course, you can hope for things as much as you want, doesn’t mean that it will happen though, but out of the nine top half v bottom half matches taking place only Colchester United, Port Vale and Fleetwood of the bottom half teams achieved victories. Roch In the weekends League 2 games, which were all on the tele because of the international window, Exeter hung on to beat Cheltenham by one goal to nil in the early game and then, because Joe Comper works for Gillingham and Jay Williams plays for Colchester, I decided to watch that one and of course, was cheering on the Kent side. In all the matches taking place there appears to be an almost top half versus bottom half feel to the fixtures and, because of the predicament we are currently in.

I have to say it would have been really good if the results had gone to form. Jay missed a sitter for the team from Essex in the first half, then got booked for a very robust tackle, which, if it had been committed in a red shirt would probably have got him sent off. Two goals in the second half saw the team I wanted to lose, win their first game in ten so now it was down to the others to perform to my script. Rochdale, Swindon, Bristol Rovers and Oldham all lost, and the Cobblers drew at Salford and Newport drew at Crewe after leading by two goals to nil.

For those of us with short memories, who can’t remember a season where we have started so badly, we need only go back to last year when we sat on exactly the same number of points after the first 12 league games played. We have scored more this season, by three goals, but unfortunately have conceded more as well. In order to ensure we stay in the football league for next season everyone knows we need to start winning games and that is why, as supporters we need to do what it says on the tin and support the lads wearing our colours through all the games left this season. Last year in the next 14 games we won just 10 more points and in the whole season we won just eight games and still managed to survive on the last day of the season.

Hopefully, although Priestley Farquharson appears to be out of contention for a while because of the injury sustained in the defeat at Wimborne, the return of Josh Flint and the arrival of Ben Heneghan will strengthen our defence and Duke-McKenna will add some Guianan magic and start scoring goals for the Red Devils again like he did against Bromley back at the beginning of October and before you know it we’ll be climbing the league ladder to safety.

Can we do it?  Yes, we can, but it must start with us making sure we beat the teams around us rather than those destined at least for the play offs. Don’t get me wrong, I would gladly take three points off the likes of Barnet next Tuesday but the minimum we should expect is for a concerted effort from all those who play for or support this club of ours. Hopefully we will achieve our first home league win here on Saturday against Fleetwood and Kabby Tshimanga will have an off night next week and live up to my friend's opinion that he really isn’t that good.  I wouldn’t bank on that though as back in the day he also said something along the lines of “Paul Fishenden, he’ll never make a centre forward".

I’m going to sign off now, before the men in the white coats arrive, but before I do go for a well-earned Sunday dinner, I would like to say that I am giving up being an optimist for being hopeful. Have a read of the definitions below and see if you should become hopeful too.

Optimism is a generalized, passive expectation or belief that things will turn out well and that positive future outcomes are more likely than negative ones. It looks at the big picture and assumes the future will improve largely on its own, through luck, external circumstances, or the natural order of things.

Hope is an active, goal-directed motivational state. It requires acknowledging current difficulties, pain, or poor odds rather than ignoring them. Hope involves building concrete plans and agency (the personal energy and determination) to act and shape a better outcome, even when the odds are stacked against you. for

Thank you, Christina Cipriani, (Crawley URC) for showing me the light

Here endeth the sermon for this week. Noli Cedere, Never Give Up.

#1995. Gary Lineker makes bleak Mauricio Pochettino prediction after Man Utd appointment

Gary Lineker insisted he would be ‘surprised’ to see Mauricio Pochettino last more than 18 months at Old Trafford following his appointment as Manchester United manager.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, with his first game in charge set to be away to Liverpool on Sunday 22 November.

The Argentine will join United after his final two matches with the United States national team, and will be tasked with bringing an immediate turnaround in the club’s form.

The Red Devils currently sit 18th in the table and are without a win in their last eight Premier League matches, a run that dates back to late August.

And while Lineker can see Pochettino arresting that slide in the short term, he fears the setup at Old Trafford will mean the Argentine will ultimately fail in a similar way to his predecessors.

#1994. Hearts sporting director addresses January transfer plans, ‘unprecedented’ injuries and recent form

Sporting director Graeme Jones has pinpointed European football and a new playing style among the key reasons for Hearts' "unprecedented" injury situation.

The Tynecastle side were missing 11 first-team players for most recent match - a 5-2 home defeat by Falkirk before the international break - and then lost another when Malachi Fagan-Walcott limped off.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The absences have coincided with a run of just one win in eight matches across all competitions, leaving Wouter Vrancken's side fourth in the Scottish Premiership and 32nd in the Uefa Conference League.

"I need to look beyond the bad luck theory and dig into possible circumstances or reasons as to why we find ourselves where we are," Jones said in a club interview. "We've got a new head coach that's brought in an intended new front foot style philosophy of how we play. We have new players who are adapting to a more competitive league than what they've been used to previously.

"We have European football which is becoming the standard we want every season but the demands that Thursday-Sunday brings on the team. And then there's also the part of the bad luck which is we've suffered a huge amount of contact injuries so far this season, more in this short period than the whole of last season.

"So, unfortunate as it is, it's a convergence of all these factors. But I also think it's important to realise that there is light at the end of the tunnel. We have players returning for the game coming up on Saturday [away to Dundee].

"We're hoping to have up to six, maybe even seven players possibly back into contention for first team training. Whether they're included in the squad, it just might be too soon, but we'll manage that accordingly. I can be confident that things are going to improve in the second half of the season, I've got no doubts on that."

Jones reassured fans that Hearts are "not sitting on our hands" with regards to addressing their injury issues.

He added: "We conducted an external review of our performance area at the turn of this year. We utilised one of the top performance practitioners in the the UK and he conducted an in-depth review that came with a numerous recommendations of things that we needed to improve. We've implemented all of these things.

"We have invested heavily in our medical department and even though it might not feel like it from the outside looking in, we're in a much better place to deal with this unprecedented level of injuries than we would have been a year ago."

Hearts came into the campaign looking to build on last season's runners-up finish in the Scottish Premiership after narrowly missing out on a first title in 66 years to Celtic on the final day. However, after 12 matches, they have collected 10 points less than they had at the same stage last season with 12 more goals conceded. They also lost their 18-month unbeaten home record against Falkirk and were beaten by rivals Hibs at Hampden for the first time in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup.

"It's not been good enough," Jones admitted. "I know that, Wouter knows that, the players know that and we're doing everything during this international week to recalibrate and rest and put things right as best we can.

"It's important to have the big picture in mind when you're in my role and looking towards the future. But I totally understand the short-term results have a massive effect on the general harmony across the board, particularly with our fans.

"I would never sit here and tell fans to be patient and calm during these periods. I am a fan, I've sat in the stand during some of the worst times throughout the club's history so I do understand. But we as a club and me as the sporting director have to remain focused on the objectives and the long-term future of the club and the success of the club that we are striving for."

Addressing Hearts' plans for the January transfer window, Jones, who was appointed sporting director two years ago, said the focus would be on balancing the squad.

"We've got a very large squad with double figures number of players that are unavailable recently so as they return back we will naturally have to look at creating balance within the squad," he said. "So we will look to decrease the size of the squad but also only add with quality. So it will be an active window like all transfer windows are but as we all know January is notoriously difficult.

"We've got plenty of evidence in the last two years that the players that sign in January don't always come in and hit the ground running. So we have to focus our attentions on the quality that can make a difference but we will be very much looking to create a bit of balance within the squad. Once all our players come back are fit and available and then looking to add quality and also help people move on that aren't getting the opportunities."

#1992. ‘Needs to move on’ – Mauricio Pochettino urged to sell £47m Manchester United star

Mauricio Pochettino has been urged to wield the axe and ‘move on’ club captain Bruno Fernandes in one of his first acts as the new Manchester United manager.

Pochettino will take charge of the United States’ two games against Haiti before beginning life as United boss after signing a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick.

And the Argentine will not have much time to work with the squad before his first Premier League match in charge of the Red Devils away to Liverpool on November 22.

Pochettino might be hopeful that the January transfer window might offer him the chance to reshape his squad after a disappointing summer transfer window left several holes in United’s squad.

And former Red Devils assistant manager Rene Meulensteen has suggested that Pochettino consider cashing in on Fernandes after his sluggish start to the season.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘In terms of Bruno, Bruno has been a fantastic servant for Manchester United over many, many years,’ Meulensteen told talkSPORT.

‘He’s not hit the same levels this year round. I think he’s also been, to some extent, maybe even mentally damaged by all the negativity that has surrounded the club and himself.

‘To be fairly honest, I think he’s been a great servant, but I would not be too sad if he decided to leave the club.

‘I think there’s many more people, more players that I think need to move on, and we need to create a different kind of dynamism in the team.’

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Fernandes won the PFA Players’ Player of the Year last year after a superb second half of the season under Carrick, but has not hit those same heights so far this campaign.

The 32-year-old is out of contract at the end of the season, with The Athletic reporting that the midfielder recently turned down a second contract offer from the club.

Fernandes can talk to foreign clubs about a potential free transfer from January, but United do have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until the summer of 2028.

The Red Devils are also said to be considering a move for talented Como midfielder Nico Paz if they do decide to part ways with Fernandes in the coming months.

#1991. What channel is Switzerland v Scotland? TV and live stream for Nations League clash

A Scotland side still finding their feet under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli conclude their Nations League B1 campaign on Monday night when they face group winners Switzerland in St Gallen.

Pocognoli earned the first home win of his tenure at the third attempt on Friday with a 2-1 win over North Macedonia but the unconvicing performance suggested the Belgian still has work to do to get the best out of his squad.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Switzerland have already secured automatic promotion to Nations League A after collecting 13 points from their five matches thus far, including a 3-0 win over 10-man Scotland at Hampden on September 29.

But while the hosts can relax, the game is not a dead rubber for Scotland, who can still claim a runners-up finish in the section with what would be a famous away victory over the side ranked 12th in the Fifa world rankings - 31 places above them.

The game is also hugely significant for captain Andy Robertson who will become Scotland’s most capped player, eclipsing Kenny Dalglish by reaching 103 appearances, if he plays on the night as expected.

Scotland will only finish second in Group B1 if they beat the Swiss and Slovenia fail to collect three points against North Macedonia in Skopje. Slovenia, on eight points, are one point ahead of Scotland in the standings but have a superior head-to-head record after their 2-1 win at Hampden last month that will see them claim the higher spot in the table if the sides finish on the same number of points.

Second place for Scotland would secure a Nations League promotion play-off in March against one of the third-placed teams from a Group A section. It would also guarantee pot two seeding for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, which takes place next month. If Scotland finish third in Nations League B1, they will drop into pot three and face high-ranking teams in pots one and two.

The Nations League B1 fixture between Switzerland and Scotland takes place at Berit Sitterstadion in St. Gallen on Monday, November 16, 2026. Kick-off is 7.45pm.

The match will be broadcast live on BBC 2 and the BBC Scotland channel with coverage starting at 7.30pm.

The game can be live streamed for free on the BBC Sport website and the BBC iPlayer.

Scotland picked up no fresh injury concerns against North Macedonia on Friday but head coach Sebastien Pocognoli is expected to make changes. “I will need to consider the best approach for the game regarding the quality and also the fitness of some players,” he said. “We have some players in the squad who we have to manage. They cannot play two games in a row.”

Switzerland, meanwhile, are expected to rotate their squad. Head coach Murat Yakin will be without Internazionale defender Manuel Akanji, captain Granit Xhaka of Sunderland, Aston Villa's Johan Manzambi and Nottingham Forest winger Dan Ndoye. Yakin revealed that 20-year-old Sion striker Winsley Boteli will earn his fourth senior cap, while 23-year-old Young Boys midfielder Alvyn Sanches will be handed his seventh, both from the start.

The entire officiating team is from the Netherlands with referee Danny Makkelie taking charge on the field. He is joined by assistant referees Hessel Steegstra and Jan de Vries, with Alex Bos acting as the fourth official. Erwin Blank serves as the Video Assistant Referee (VAR), who will be joined in the VAR booth by Jeroen Manschot.

#1989. Ex-Premier League ref calls Mikel Arteta a ‘nightmare’ to deal with

Former Premier League referee Graham Scott has named Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as the toughest person to deal with on the touchline.

Last month, Arteta received his second yellow card of the season during Arsenal’s 2-0 win over Everton but said after the game that he had a dossier of other managers committing similar offences which have gone unpunished.

The Arsenal manager now faces a one-match touchline ban if he receives a third yellow card.

Scott, who refereed in the Premier League for a decade before retiring in 2025, claims Arteta ‘does push all the limits all of the time’ and described the Spaniard as ‘hard work’.

When asked who was the worst manager to deal with on the touchline, Scott told The Athletic: ‘Well, the trite answer is all of them when they’re losing.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘The honest answer, I’m afraid, I know whatever I say at this point just gets me pelters but it is Arteta. He is the hardest work.

‘He really does push all the limits all of the time. I don’t mind that in many ways, he’s trying to get a competitive advantage for his team. That’s fine. That’s part of his job. And of course, he’s entitled to do it, and it’s for us to place them, but he does make your life extremely difficult.

‘He’s out of his box [technical area] all the time. I watched him recently in the game against Everton and every time Everton had the ball anywhere near the touchline on his side, he was like joining in the press, his toes are on the touchline.

‘As fourth official, it’s a nightmare, because if you step forward and do anything about it, you’re being pedantic, being petty. He does get away with rather too much. The officials do need to be a bit tighter. And I was one of them who let him do that. I’m not going to deny that. But he was just hard work. Really, really hard work all the time in a way that others tended to be hard work some of the time.

#1988. When did Scotland last beat Switzerland? Full head to head record and last five games

Scotland’s Nations League campaign wraps up on Monday evening with a tough encounter against Switzerland as the side aims to snatch an unlikely promotion playoff spot in Group B1 from Slovenia.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli finally got his first home win with a 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday, and now his team will look to make it back-to-back wins for the first time under his management while hoping Slovenia slip up in the group’s other game.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, should Scotland fail to win in St Gallen, hopes of promotion back to League A will be extinguished. A third-place finish will also have ramifications for the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifiers, which are drawn in Belfast this December.

But when did Scotland last beat Switzerland? What is their head-to-head record, and when did they last meet? Here’s everything you need to know about Scotland’s record against Switzerland.

The teams have faced each other a total of 18 times, and have met twice in major tournament finals, with both encounters taking place in the group stage of the European Championships.

They last faced each other just last month in the Nations League, where Switzerland ran out 3-0 winners after Jack Hendry was sent off early on at Hampden Park. Prior to that game, they drew 1-1 at Euro 2024 in Germany, with Scott McTominay opening the scoring early on for Scotland, before Xherdan Shaqiri equalised shortly afterwards.

From their 18 games played, Scotland have eight wins, giving them a 33.3% win percentage. Switzerland have won a total of six times - a 22.22 per cent win percentage. A further four games have ended in a draw.

Despite having the better head to head record against the Swiss, the Scotland men’s national team have not tasted victory against them for over 30 years. Their most recent win came at Euro 1996 at Villa Park, Birmingham on 18 June, where they earned their first win a 1-0 win in their final group game at the tournament.

The victory came via a fine strike from Ally McCoist in the 36th minute, but was not enough for Scotland to qualify for the knockout stages of the tournament, with the Netherlands finishing above them on goal difference. The Switzerland side that day included future Celtic defender Ramon Vega.

Scotland line up that night: Andy Goram, Tom Boyd, Colin Calderwood, Colin Hendry, Stuart McCall, Gary McAllister, John Collins, Tosh McKinlay (Scott Booth, 60), Craig Burley, Gordon Durie and Ally McCoist (John Spencer, 84).

29 September 2026: Scotland 0-3 Switzerland (Nations League)

19 June 2024: Scotland 1-1 Switzerland (Euro 2024)

1 March 2006: Scotland 1-3 Switzerland (Friendly)

18 June 1996: Scotland 1-0 Switzerland (Euro 1996)

8 September 1993: Scotland 1-1 Switzerland (World Cup 1994 Qualifier)

With an international break hitting the top-tier domestic game - and on a stunning bright, but cold, late autumn day - the Pirates’ biggest crowd of the season, 226, gathered at the Polegrove to see if Jay Skinner-Swain’s men could kick on with their impressive league campaign to date.

Early signs were encouraging. Ash Latuske, wide on the right, was impressive from the off and on just three minutes he opened the scoring. Jack Shonk brought down a high ball and squared it to Latuske in space in the box and he grabbed the chance to knock it in.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Seaford Town have had a mixed few months of league action but have managed to chalk up some decent results and they now set about trying to claw their way back into the game after the early setback. They opened up a decent chance on 25 minutes but Finn Holter in the Bexhill goal reacted sharply to make a good save.

Minutes later Theo Coombs came close to doubling the Pirates lead, his shot heading wide of the post after he was well set up by Ryan Moir from out on the left.

As the play shifted quickly back down the other end, the pendulum swung again as a Charlie Playford challenge was adjudged by the ref to warrant a penalty. There were few complaints and the Seaford man crashed the ball home to level the score.

It was disappointing for Bexhill, but the team picked themselves up and got back at it straight from the restart. The run-up to half-time saw a period of sustained Pirates pressure.

On 40 minutes Luke Donaldson struck an absolute peach of a volley which Josh Mitchell-Lake in the Seaford goal managed to get just enough of a touch on to divert it over the bar.

That was followed shortly after by an acrobatic volley from defender Dale Penn which just cleared the bar with the Polegrove willing it in as Penn continues his search for that elusive goal.

One all at half-time meant that there was plenty to do.

Coombs has developed a knack in recent weeks of scoring quality goals at crucial moments. Saturday added another to that tally. On 65 minutes he picked up the ball outside the box, surged forwards and drove home a quality finish from distance.

But there was plenty of action and controversy left in this contest and half an hour into the half the ref handed Donaldson a straight red for a first offence that he viewed as dangerous.

Bexhill had played a large chunk of their away game at Seaford with ten men in August and it seemed to inspire them then. Now it had the same effect.

Suddenly Bexhill shirts were everywhere, winning the ball and setting up a wave of attacks. The Pirates made that pressure count with sheer persistence from Shonk creating a chance for himself that he squeezed home from a tight angle.

As Seaford tried to make some use of their one-man advantage they were leaving large gaps at the back for Bexhill to exploit with Moir in particular making hay.

Just after the 90 minutes were up he drove a shot towards goal and, with the keeper out of position, a defender threw himself across the line and handled to stop a certain goal. Off he went with a red card and Shonk blasted in the spot kick.

Deep into injury time Moir came close to nailing the goal he deserved. Breaking clear, shrugging off a challenge and just failed to beat the keeper.

This was a great result for Bexhill in front of a bumper crowd and they aim to keep the momentum going with another home league clash against Midhurst and Easebourne on Saturday.

#1985. Scotland year that started with promise ends in another setback amid fears over one player’s career

A year that started so full of promise for Scotland ground to a humiliating halt in St Gallen. The 13th match of a World Cup dominated 12 months always threatened to be the toughest of tough tasks.

Not perhaps as challenging as taking on Brazil in Miami or Morocco in Boston. But Switzerland, World Cup quarter-finalists themselves, are no pushovers, as they proved in a match of supposedly little consequence for them. Having already secured top place in Group B1, they enjoyed the luxury of making changes and still eased to a deserved 4-0 victory in the university city.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

What did Sebastien Pocognoli learn? Not too much as he watched his side picked apart by Murat Yakin’s exciting team. Two goals just after the break – a tap in from Winsley Boteli and a rocket from Alvyn Sanches – rendered the second half little more than a training exercise.

Substitute Zeki Amdouni wrapped things up in the final minute with a shot from the edge of the of the box that took a wicked deflection off Luke Graham. It was that kind of night. Lewis Ferguson had put through his own goal to set the Swiss on their way after 22 minutes.

It was anything but the much-needed statement result for Pocognoli some had surmised might be possible against hosts who could afford to coast. Instead, there were fears that Switzerland – 3-0 up after just 51 minutes – would pile on the pain.

Scotland suffered a 7-0 defeat against Uruguay 80 or so miles away in Basel at the 1954 World Cup and something as embarrassing felt possible, particularly when the "oles" from the home fans were ringing around the Sitterstadion early in the second half.

This wasn’t how Andy Robertson, who had 103 stitched into the tongues of his boots, wanted to become Scotland’s most-capped ever men’s player. Scotland were completely licked.

Sanches missed an open goal with eight minutes left after Angus Gunn miscued a pass, although the Swiss forward was around 50 yards out. The keeper did well to block a later shot from the same player but was helpless when Amdouni’s deflected effort looped into the net for 4-0.

Of course, it helps when the opposition scores the all-important first goal for you. Ferguson inadvertently put through his own net as he attempted to cut out the danger following Zachary Athekame’s cross from the right. Not too long afterwards, about 900 miles away in Skopje, Slovenia scored their opener against North Macedonia to further put the Scots behind the black ball in their quest to finish in second place. The Slovenians ended up winning 3-0, leaving Scotland in a very distant third place in the group and wondering what the future holds. At least there are no more games until March. It’s been a tough old year. The memorable moments have almost all occurred off the pitch. It isn’t all on Pocognoli, granted.

What was underlined here is that the Belgian could do with a bit of fortune. He could do with the stars aligning in the way they did for Steve Clarke a year ago this week, when everything seemed to fall into place eventually on a night of nights against Denmark in Glasgow.

Pocognoli, by contrast, is struggling to get going. His Hampden bow against Switzerland was ruined by Jack Hendry’s red card just ten minutes in. Here he saw Scott McTominay blaze over from six yards and watched John McGinn place a header straight into the hands of keeper Yvon Mvogo.

More serious woe arrived in the form of the latest injury misery to befall Aaron Hickey. The former Hearts player’s left hamstring has proved troublesome for a few managers, including Clarke, and obviously for the player himself.

It was heartbreaking to see the player stumble having performed a typically diligent defensive duty, in this case mopping up by directing a header into Gunn’s arms. He also pulled something in the process and made a sad exit down the tunnel after 36 minutes, with Nathan Patterson replacing him. Brentford will be furious although it’s not as if Pocognoli hadn’t sought to manage the player’s minutes.

He left him out of the first game of the window against North Macedonia. This latest setback feels bigger than just what it means for Pocognoli and Scotland. It raises real fears about a brilliant young player’s career.

So the outcome of the match, as dispiriting as the defeat was, needs to be placed in context. It might have proved a happier evening had Hickey’s header from Andy Robertson’s cross 24 minutes sneaked in rather than past the post just minutes after Ferguson’s own goal horror.

Hickey was also in the thick of things after a clever touch from Oli McBurnie saw him burst into the Swiss half. Kieran Tierney was to his left and was screaming to be played in but the wing-back just could not get the ball out of his feet and the chance was gone.

Ferguson’s misery was all the more frustrating because it was so unnecessary. Ryan Porteous was waiting to clear but the Bologna midfielder got in before him and steered past Gunn while attempting to clear the danger.

The game was over six minutes into the second half. Ballet exchanged passes with Remo Feuler and shot towards goal. Although Boteli probably didn’t need to help the ball over the line, he did anyway at the risk of seeing the goal chalked off for offside.

He was just onside and was credited with the strike. There was no doubt who scored the third for the hosts, with Sanches latching on to a loose ball after Patterson had been dispossessed before rifling into the corner past Gunn.

The loss of a fourth goal seemed inconsequential but did seem to sum everything up. These are very different times to 12 months ago and more hurt may lie ahead.

“Matt has been outstanding for us recently, but I thought everyone put in a tremendous shift. The second goal came when we were pushing to get something from the game, which was frustrating.

“The performances are certainly improving, and the lads deserve enormous credit for their attitude and commitment. However, we can't keep talking about playing well and coming away with nothing.
