#1924. Martin Zubimendi stance on Chelsea transfer as Arsenal set asking price

Martin Zubimendi is seriously considering leaving Arsenal for the first time and has refused to rule out a move to Chelsea, according to reports in Spain.

Zubimendi is yet to start a Premier League game for Arsenal this season, with the concerning lack of game-time sparking speculation over his future at the Emirates Stadium.

The Spanish midfielder enjoyed a bright start to his Gunners career following a £60m move from Real Sociedad, earning rave reviews from Mikel Arteta this time last year.

But Zubimendi had lost his place in the Arsenal team by the end of the season, with a teenage Myles Lewis-Skelly instead starting the Champions League final against PSG.

The 27-year-old has continued to struggle for minutes this season and is now, for the first time, considering his future at the club.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

Spanish outlet AS say Zubimendi has his eye on a January exit and is ‘open to everything’ following reports linking him with Chelsea, Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid.

Xabi Alonso is keen to strengthen his midfield options and knows Zubimendi well from his previous spell at Real Sociedad.

Zubimendi is contracted to Arsenal until 2030 but reports in Spain say the north London club will consider offers for the World Cup winner of at least £60m.

Last week, Zubimendi was forced to address speculation linking him with a move away from Arsenal while on international duty with Spain.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘To be honest, I’m sometimes surprised by the press too,’ he told Marca. ‘I understand that the winter transfer window is approaching and rumours can surface, but I think we need to be a bit more careful with what we publish.

‘Ultimately, everyone has a team they play for, and we need to respect that. I’ve also read that I might be close, but not at all.

‘Often a news story comes out and it seems that if it doesn’t come true, it’s quickly forgotten and nothing happens.

‘I’m learning how this world works and getting used to it, but sometimes I could avoid a lot of the messages I receive because of this kind of news.’

Zubimendi also revealed he was warned about a possible lack of minutes by Arteta ahead of the 2026/27 campaign.

Arteta bolstered his midfield options over the summer, with Arsenal spending £75m to sign Brazil international Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United.

‘I spoke with Mikel at the beginning of the season,’ Zubimendi added. ‘As he does with all the players, he explained the plan to me.

‘He warned me that there were new signings and that there would be playing time for everyone. And here we are, fighting for it.

‘I understand because, for me, we’re among the five best teams in Europe. There are some fantastic players. New signings have arrived in my position, and there were already some very good players.

‘I’m also part of that competition that makes it so difficult to get playing time. I’m calm and happy with how I’m handling this situation.

‘It’s something I’ve never experienced before, and I think you learn from these situations too. Besides, it’s in moments like these that you need the people around you the most, and they’re there for you.

‘I’m patient. When you’ve been playing a lot of minutes and your role changes to not playing as much, I’m able to see the positive side.

‘I think everything passes, that just like last year the opposite happened to me and I played practically everything, this can change very quickly.’

#1921. Prediction: Wales vs Portugal

Portugal travel to Cardiff on Tuesday night knowing that avoiding defeat against Wales will be enough to guarantee first place in UEFA Nations League Group A4.

While the visitors have already secured their place in the quarter-finals, Wales are facing a very different battle. Craig Bellamy’s side are certain to finish bottom of the group, but a point could prove crucial in helping them secure a place in the relegation playoffs.

Wales head into their final group match on the back of a disappointing 3-1 defeat away to Norway, a result that ended any lingering hopes of climbing the standings.

Bellamy’s side had known that a draw in Oslo would have kept them in third position, but the loss confirmed that they would finish behind Portugal, Denmark and Norway in Group A4.

However, there is still something to play for. The Dragons remain in a strong position to secure a relegation playoff berth, and avoiding defeat against Portugal would strengthen their chances considerably.

Recent form has been a concern, though. Wales have won just one of their last nine matches, recording three draws and five defeats since March. Despite those struggles, Bellamy will hope that home advantage can help his side finish the campaign on a positive note.

Ethan Ampadu is suspended and will miss the match, with Josh Sheehan expected to replace him in midfield.

Connor Roberts is likely to come into the side at right-back after Neco Williams suffered an injury.

David Brooks could also be rewarded for his goal against Norway, with Bellamy considering changes in attacking areas.

Portugal’s hopes of finishing top of the group remain firmly in their own hands despite suffering a surprise setback at the weekend.

Jorge Jesus’s side were heavily beaten 4-1 at home by Denmark, a result that ended a four-match winning streak in the Nations League. Portugal found themselves four goals behind before eventually finding the net late in the contest.

The defeat was particularly disappointing given the momentum they had built following Cristiano Ronaldo’s international retirement. Prior to the Denmark game, Portugal had won all four of their group matches, including a 1-0 victory over Wales on matchday one. Jesus expectedly had to answer some uncomfortable questions after the game.

Even so,  Portugal are still, realistically, the favourites to finish top of the group. A draw or victory in Cardiff would ensure Denmark cannot overtake them on the final day.

One slight concern for Jesus is that the only clean sheet of his tenure so far came in that opening victory against Wales.

Ruben Dias is suspended and unavailable, meaning Antonio Silva is expected to move into the centre of defence.

Nazinho is an option if Portugal decide to rotate their full-back positions.

Joao Neves and Bernardo Silva could both be recalled to the starting lineup, while Ruben Neves and Pedro Neto may drop to the bench.

Both teams will be looking to respond after disappointing results at the weekend, but Portugal appear better equipped to do so.

Wales have struggled for consistency throughout the campaign and continue to find victories difficult to come by. Portugal, meanwhile, have already shown their superiority in this fixture and possess significantly more quality across the pitch.

The visitors may not have everything their own way in Cardiff, but they should have enough to end the group stage with a victory and secure first place.

Prediction: Flamengo vs Athletico Paranaense

#1920. Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1. However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs2,3. Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

The global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies. Among these, tidal energy presents a uniquely predictable and substantial resource. Unlike other renewables such as wind and solar, tidal currents are governed by an astronomical cycle, which offers a consistent and forecastable power source4,5. The scale of this resource is significant. Tidal power is estimated at 50 TW h yr−1 in Europe6 and as much as 220 TW h yr−1 in the USA alone7. Near-term deployment targets are 1 GW by 2035 in the UK3, with international roadmaps project deployments eventually exceeding 300 GW worldwide by 20508. These highlight the potential of tidal energy in contributing to energy security and renewable energy portfolios.

Despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an important barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source. A primary challenge is the hydrodynamic load fluctuations that arise from large variations in flow velocity, turbulence, turbine yaw with respect to the incoming stream, velocity shear along the water depth2, wave-induced oscillating currents9, and wake interaction within turbine arrays10. These fluctuating loads are a primary design consideration and are associated with accelerated fatigue, reduced operational lifespans and unplanned downtime. These reliability concerns result in blade and turbine designs with high capital costs, which directly increase the levelized cost of energy (LCOE)3.

To address the challenge of the dynamic loads, various mitigation strategies have been developed. Active control typically deploys systems to actively regulate the pitch11 or camber12 of the blades, therefore, to regulate power output, control mean loads and improve start-up performance. Although the active control systems are effective in certain operational envelopes, the reliability of sophisticated sensors and actuators in the harsh undersea environment remains a concern. Furthermore, the response times of the activator limit effectiveness against rapid, high-frequency load fluctuations13,14.

To address these concerns, there has been an increased focus on developing passive control mechanisms. Passive control is mainly realized in two ways: introducing changes in the blade pitch or modifying the blade camber. Passive pitch control involves designing blades that can rotate around their spanwise axis in response to changing hydrodynamic loads, thereby altering their angle of attack. This is typically achieved by incorporating a pre-loaded torsional spring mechanism at the blade root. Theoretical work in refs. 15,16 are among the first to introduce the concept. Both demonstrated that complete cancellation of the load fluctuation is possible without compromising the mean power. This is followed by a numerical study in ref. 17, which confirmed more than 80% load fluctuations can be reduced in sheared flow conditions, with additional benefits such as faster wake recovery, which improves turbine array performance. Reference 18 has contributed a general framework for the design of passive pitching systems, identifying the locations of the pivot point for maximizing load mitigation. Experimental validations in ref. 19 have confirmed the ability of passive pitching systems in the reduction of time-averaged loadings.

Passive pitching systems are effective for low-frequency, large-scale adjustments and power regulation by adjusting the global angle of attack of the blades. However, the added inertia due to the displacement of the pitching axis required by effective pitching systems, as well as the bearing friction, limits the response of the system to high-frequency disturbances, such as turbulent eddies or rapid shear variations. Moreover, despite being simpler than active control systems, passive pitch blades still introduce extra moving parts and potential failure points in harsh undersea environments. Research has identified that for wind turbine applications, most of the failures originate from the pitch system20, highlighting the significant operational advantage of a robust, passive design.

An alternative design philosophy can be found in nature, where organisms from fish to trees passively reconfigure their shape through distributed material compliance to manage fluid dynamic forces21,22. Drawing from these biological principles, passive morphing flexible blades offer an alternative strategy, where flexibility is distributed along the blade, allowing each blade section to adapt automatically through fluid–structure interaction. Therefore, a faster response time can be achieved with a fixed-pitch blade that does not require hinges and bearings. Passive morphing blades are common in wind energy applications23,24, in which the blade twists to feather in response to a wind gust. This technique, known as aeroelastic tailoring, requires ad hoc structural design, whose scalability and reliability for large tidal turbines is yet to be demonstrated. In fact, for similar power-rated turbines, the bending moment experienced by tidal turbines is higher than that of wind turbines. Therefore, the need for a scalable, reliable, passive system that can mitigate both rapid, localized turbulent fluctuations and slower, large-scale changes in inflow velocity on large-scale tidal turbines remains unmet.

This study directly addresses this challenge by proposing a blade with chordwise flexibility, rather than spanwise flexibility, as in aeroelastic tailoring. The frontal and thickest part of the blade, which provides structural integrity, is rigid. Instead, the trailing edge is flexible from root to tip. Specifically, we provide the first comprehensive experimental demonstration that a carefully designed chordwise-flexible blade can achieve both control of the mean power and thrust with the quasi-steady variations of flow velocities over the tidal cycle (for example, the diurnal tidal cycle) and mitigation of the high-frequency (turbulence) hydrodynamic load fluctuations on tidal turbines, while enabling the same yield as a conventional rigid blade equipped with active pitch control. To demonstrate this potential, we experimentally evaluated the performance of these chordwise-flexible blades against a rigid baseline in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh. The turbine was tested across a range of nominal inflow velocities u∞ = 0.5–1.0 m s−1, and tip-speed ratios (λ) from 3 to 9, with the flexible blades designed for optimal performance at u∞ ≈ 0.85 m s−1. Our analysis first addresses the low-frequency load mitigation over a tidal cycle before examining the high-frequency load fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms of the deformation of the blade. Overall, we demonstrated a new pathway to enhance turbine reliability and survivability, reducing capital costs associated with the active pitch system, and reducing maintenance costs by removing hinges, bearings and actuators, ultimately reducing the LCOE.

The structural design of a tidal turbine is primarily dictated by low-frequency loads, which, in this context, refers to the quasi-steady hydrodynamic loads that change as the mean inflow velocity varies over a tidal cycle. To investigate the potential for load control in this regime, the time-averaged performance of the flexible blades was compared against a rigid baseline. Figure 1 shows the time-averaged power (CP), thrust (CT), and root bending moment (CM) coefficients as a function of tip-speed ratio λ, at all tested inflow velocities. The results demonstrate that the introduction of blade flexibility does not compromise the primary function of energy capture of the turbine. As shown in Fig. 1a, at the rated velocity (uR = 0.878 m s−1) and above, the power coefficient of the flexible blade closely matches that of the rigid blade, achieving a comparable peak CP of approximately 0.37. Notably, the limited value of the maximum CP of both the rigid and flexible blades compared with full-scale state-of-the-art turbines is due to the low Reynolds number at which the model-scale turbines were tested (Methods).

The key advantage of the flexible blade design is its ability to passively regulate peak loadings. At the rated velocity, the thrust coefficient of the flexible blade is comparable to that of the rigid blade near the optimal power-producing tip-speed ratio (λ ≈ 5.5−6), as shown in Fig. 1b. However, the performance of the flexible blades diverges from rigid ones for λ values beyond this optimal range. This high λ region is typically explored by the turbine control strategy to cap power when inflow velocity exceeds the rated velocity. Under these conditions, the flexible blade thrust passively decreases, whereas the rigid one increases. This demonstrates a load-shedding mechanism that can protect the turbine structure during the most demanding high-flow conditions and will be discussed in detail in the next section, in which we simulate the power and thrust a tidal turbine experiences over a tidal cycle. However, at off-design conditions, the flexible blade exhibits higher CT and CM values than at its design speed. While this results in higher thrust coefficients at lower velocities, the absolute forces, which scale with velocity squared (\(F\propto {u}_{\infty }^{2}\)), are much smaller during lower flow periods and are not as important for the structural design of the turbine as the peak loads experienced at or above rated velocity. Therefore, the ability of the flexible blade technology to match power performance while simultaneously offering a passive mechanism to reduce the most important structural loads represents a marked advancement for designing more durable and cost-effective tidal turbines.

a–c, Time-averaged coefficients of power (a), thrust (b) and root bending moment (c) as a function of the tip-speed ratio for rigid and flexible blades at different flow speeds.

To quantify the practical benefits of the passive load mitigation of the chordwise-flexible blade in realistic inflow, we simulate the performance over a representative tidal cycle and compare it against a rigid blade turbine with the same control strategy and a state-of-the-art, actively pitch-controlled turbine (see Supplementary Note 2 for modelling of the active pitch-and-speed control turbine). The sinusoidal inflow velocity represents the flow seen by a tidal turbine during a tidal cycle is shown in Fig. 2a, which is

a–d, Time history over a simulated tidal period of the freestream speed (a), the quasi-steady power (b), the tip-speed ratio (c) and the quasi-steady thrust (d). Data are presented for a rigid-blade turbine with only an active speed controller, a state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed controller, and rubber blades with an active speed controller. All data are divided by the corresponding rated value.

The cut-in velocity of the turbine is selected at u∞/uR = 0.2. The turbine operates at λ = 5.5 when the velocity is lower than rated. At the rated speed, all turbine configurations are operated at the same tip-speed ratio (λR) and provide the same quasi-steady power (PR) and thrust (TR). At higher than rated velocities, λ is such that P/PR = 1. The maximum velocity is set at u∞/uR = 1.2, representative of typical tidal turbine operating conditions.

The simulation first confirms that the passive design of the flexible blade does not compromise its primary function of energy capture. The normalized power profiles shown in Fig. 2b coincide for the rubber blade with speed control and the state-of-the-art active pitch control turbine, where the turbine speed is shown in Fig. 2c. As the total energy harvested is proportional to the integral of the power curves over the tidal cycle, the overlap of the curves confirms a negligible difference in overall energy yield. This demonstrates that the load-mitigation benefits of flexible blades can be achieved without a penalty to energy capture in a real-world setting.

The advantage of the flexible blade design is revealed by the differences in the quasi-steady thrust (Fig. 2d) between the turbine configurations. The state-of-the-art active pitch system limits structural loads by actively feathering the blades into the flow while maintaining the rated rotational speed. For a rigid blade, using only an overspeed-control strategy, the fixed geometry cannot adapt to the increasing flow; solely increasing the tip-speed ratio results in an increasing thrust that peaks at approximately 1.65 times the rated value (Fig. 2c). By contrast, with a comparable speed-control strategy, the passive system of the flexible blade achieves the same quasi-steady power and similar quasi-steady thrust as the active control.

It is also important to note that flexible blades show a slightly higher thrust coefficient at lower, off-design velocities (Fig. 1b) than the baseline rigid blade. However, the absolute thrust force, which scales with velocity squared, is smaller during these periods than the peak values over the tidal cycle. As the maximum loading dictates the primary structural design requirements of a turbine, the nearly identical peak thrust of the passive flexible blade to that of the complex, state-of-the-art active pitch system suggests comparable outcomes for turbine longevity and maintenance costs, representing a marked advancement towards more durable and cost-effective tidal energy systems. Overall, these results indicate that the chordwise-flexible blades can offer a compelling and robust alternative to the state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed control turbine system.

An effective passive system must also address high-frequency load fluctuations, which are a primary driver of fatigue damage. In this context, high frequency refers to the unsteady load components that occur at frequencies of the order of the period of revolution, such as those induced by turbulence, velocity shear or wake interaction, and so on. Figure 3 quantifies the effectiveness of the flexible blades by presenting the standard deviation of load fluctuations relative to the reference rigid blades at rated velocity. To reflect realistic conditions over a tidal cycle, the data for u∞/uR ≤ 1 are presented at the optimal tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5) for maximum power extraction, whereas the data for conditions above the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06) are presented at the higher tip-speed ratio (λ = 8) that is used to cap power. Figure 3 shows a substantial reduction of unsteady loads for all three components when the turbine is operating under its most demanding conditions. At the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.0), where the turbine operates at its optimal λ for maximum power extraction, the flexible blades provide effective fluctuation reduction across power, thrust and root bending moment (mitigated by approximately 18%, 23% and 28%, respectively). Furthermore, even when the inflow velocity increases beyond the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06), the load fluctuation mitigation remains substantial. This demonstrates the powerful and robust damping ability of the flexible blades during both the maximum-power and power-capping phases of operation, when the absolute magnitude of fluctuating forces is greatest. At the lowest velocities (for example, u∞/uR = 0.51), where the blade operates in a stalled condition, fluctuations are known to increase relative to the rigid blade. However, their absolute magnitude is small, reaching only about 15–35% of the fluctuation level of the rigid blade at its rated velocity. A more detailed analysis, presented in Supplementary Note 3, confirms that this mitigation is robust across a wide range of tip-speed ratios under these high-flow conditions.

a–c, Standard deviation of power (a), thrust (b) and root-bending moment (c) of flexible and rigid blades, for the optimum tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5). All quantities are divided by those of the rigid blade at rated velocity.

To illustrate the physics of the passive load regulation mechanism demonstrated previously, the deformation of the flexible blade is visualized at the tip section. Figure 4 shows the phase-averaged digital image correlation (DIC) measurements of the tip of the same flexible blade at a constant azimuthal angle, in which the blade is horizontal with downward velocity. The successful application of this technique using fully submerged cameras represents a significant experimental achievement, as most underwater DIC studies to date have been performed through observation windows rather than submerging the camera in the fluid25. In this way, complex optical distortions and refractive index mismatches associated with viewing ports are avoided, thereby achieving a more accurate measurement. In this study, the DIC system measured the deformation of the suction side of the blade. The full blade profile was then reconstructed by adding the known thickness distribution of the undeformed blade to the measured deformed chord line.

Phase-averaged profiles of one blade tip measured with DIC when the blade span is horizontal, and the tangential velocity is pointing downwards. Coordinates x, y are normalized by the chord length at the blade tip with origin at the quarter chord.

The measurements demonstrate the mechanism of the passive morphing concept. The undeformed flexible blade was designed with a significant initial camber, noticeably higher than that of the conventional rigid blade profile. The high camber present in both the initial blade shape and the subsequent deformed shape before reaching the designed operating point is the primary reason for the higher thrust force generated by the flexible blade operating off-design. Under hydrodynamic loading, the flexible trailing edge deflects upwards, causing the entire profile to flatten into a shape with less camber. This passive feathering becomes more pronounced with higher inflow velocities, which is the mechanism that reduces the thrust coefficient at high tip-speed ratios and velocities.

DIC measurements of different blades (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2) show that blades with lower flexural rigidity undergo greater camber reduction and exhibit stronger load shedding. Specifically, for blades with the same mould geometry, a too-stiff blade results in a too-low pitch and too-high camber, and thus high mean and unsteady thrust. Conversely, a too-soft blade results in an over-pitched blade and low power capture.

The observed mean load-shedding behaviour shown in Fig. 1 arises primarily from quasi-steady passive morphing, and not from dynamic blade deformation resulting in hysteresis, vortex dynamics, and so on. DIC reconstructions of each individual blade at the same azimuthal position reveal only a narrow spread about the mean shape, corresponding to a standard deviation of the pitch variation of approximately ±0.2° (Extended Data Fig. 3).

To further verify that the mean load-shedding behaviour is due to a quasi-steady morphing, we compare the measured blade deformations (Fig. 4) and the corresponding power and thrust (Fig. 1) with those computed with an in-house fluid–structure interaction solver based on a quasi-steady low-order model (Methods). The blade shapes computed with this program are in good agreement with those measured experimentally, and so are the predicted power and thrust for different tip-speed ratios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the numerical solver assumes the blade is in static equilibrium under hydrodynamic loads, these results confirm that the governing physics is quasi-steady.

The fluid–structure interaction of the flexible blades is governed by two non-dimensional groups such as the Reynolds number (Re) and Cauchy number (Ca) (defined in the Methods). The experiments are performed at sufficiently high Re that the hydrodynamic load coefficients are about the same as those at full scale, as shown by the almost identical values for the rigid blade tested at different velocities in Fig. 1. To ensure geometric similarity between the model and the full-scale strain of the flexible blades, the Young modulus E of rubber must be scaled up to maintain the same Ca across scales. As discussed in Supplementary Note 4, rubber features a sufficiently high range of E for full-scale applications. Furthermore, rubber has the advantage of matching the mass density of water, enabling the design of buoyancy-neutral blades and preventing mass-related load fluctuations.

To demonstrate the scalability of the present results, numerical simulations are performed using the in-house fluid–structure interaction solver to model a utility-scale turbine. A rated speed of u∞ = 3.0 m s−1 and a 20-m diameter turbine is selected consistently with modern, state-of-the-art commercial turbines26 and typical energetic tidal sites27. Simulations performed at the respective Re and the same Ca confirm that power and thrust coefficient curves are similar at model and full scale (Extended Data Fig. 5), and therefore the present results are applicable to utility-scale turbines. Although E of the steel spar can be scaled up in numerical simulations, this is not possible in practice. Therefore, different full-scale spar design options are discussed in Supplementary Note 5.

Finally, rubber features high fatigue endurance. Preliminary calculations in Supplementary Note 6 show that the fatigue life of a full-scale rubber blade would substantially surpass the 20 years of service expected by state-of-the-art turbines.

Overall, by allowing similar control on power at thrust above rated speed than active pitch control systems, and mitigating load fluctuations, this technology offers a viable pathway to lower the LCOE. Furthermore, the reduction in load fluctuations enables deployment in energetic, highly turbulent sites previously deemed unviable due to the high fatigue loads. Further analysis of the potential industrial impact of this technology is presented in Supplementary Note 7.

This experimental investigation has evaluated the performance of tidal turbine flexible rubber blades with passive chordwise flexibility, compared against conventional rigid blades. Our results confirmed that the power coefficient of the flexible blade at the design tip-speed ratio is comparable to that of its rigid counterpart, demonstrating that load mitigation benefits are achieved without penalty to the primary function of the turbine as an energy harvester.

The main advantage of the flexible blades is their ability to deform, shedding the excess of load at off-design conditions. This reconfiguration allows control of power by manipulating the angular velocity of the turbine, while achieving passive mitigation of the high-frequency fluctuations that drive fatigue damage.

Therefore, the chordwise-flexible blades offer a compelling and robust alternative to state-of-the-art active pitch control. By mitigating loads with a much simpler setup, the flexible blade eliminates a significant source of potential failure and maintenance costs in offshore renewables.

The mechanism for load mitigation is confirmed through DIC measurement and a quasi-steady low-order code, which shows that the stiffness and initial geometry of the blade produce a controlled ‘feather’ as loads increase. The no-flow geometry and stiffness of the blade are designed so that, under flow conditions approaching the design point, it deforms toward the reference rigid-blade configuration.

Looking ahead, this work opens up new pathways for tidal turbine design and cost reduction. The demonstrated reductions in peak and fatigue loading could allow a reduction in structural requirements for both the blades and their supporting structure, lowering capital costs and enabling higher generator ratings, which in turn improve rated capacity per unit mass. Moreover, the increased robustness from the removal of the pitching system reduces operational and maintenance costs. These factors contribute to a lower LCOE of tidal turbines, addressing the primary barrier to the large-scale deployment of tidal energy farms. By making the technology more financially viable, this technology offers a realistic and attractive option for renewable energy production.

All experiments were conducted in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh, a circular combined wave–current basin designed for scaled testing of offshore renewable energy devices. The tank has a diameter of 25 m and, for the present campaign, was operated in current-only mode with a working water depth of 1.92 m. A schematic of the facility is shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a. The experiments were performed at six inflow velocities in the range u∞ = 0.444–0.923 m s−1, corresponding to a diameter-based Reynolds number,

from 0.49 × 106 to 1.16 × 106, where ν is the kinematic viscosity and d is the turbine diameter. See Supplementary Note 4 for a discussion on the Reynolds number scaling.

FloWave turbulence is between 8% and 9%, and integral length scales of about 25% of the water depth28. These turbulent characteristics are consistent with energetic tidal sites such as, for example, the Fall of Warness29. There, the turbulence intensity is between 5% and 11%, with integral length scales of approximately 30–50% of the channel depth. The mean vertical shear in FloWave is approximately a power law with a 1/12 exponent (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which is only slightly weaker than the 1/10 power-law profile commonly used to represent tidal flows30. Extended Data Table 1 summarizes the comparison between FloWave and the representative tidal sites.

A three-bladed horizontal-axis turbine with a rotor diameter d = 1.26 m was installed in the tank centre, at hub height zhub = 0.876 m. The turbine is equipped with a brushless d.c. motor and a 25:1 planetary gearbox. The main components of the turbine are outlined in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The results presented in the main text refer to four sets of blades: one set of rigid blades used as a baseline and three sets of rubber blades. The baseline rigid blades are CNC-machined (SS316) using a modified NACA 63-415 hydrofoil profile along the span. The profile was modified to ensure a blunt trailing edge, as specified in ref. 31. These blades exhibited negligible flapwise and edgewise deformations. Notably, utility-scale tidal turbine blades exhibit some structural compliance. However, here the model-scale rigid blade was deliberately made rigid to provide a defined geometry.

The main text presents the results for the rigid blades and one set of rubber blades with the optimal stiffness. Conversely, the Extended Data figures also include results for the other two sets of rubber blades, with higher and lower stiffness than optimal. The flexible blades were manufactured by injecting a proprietary rubber mixture into a mould and around a steel spar. All rubber blades have the same mould geometry. See Extended Data Fig. 8 for schematics of the rubber blade. The aeroelastic properties of the blade are tailored along its span by varying the ratio of the rigid spar width to the local chord length, which increases from the tip towards the root with an average of 45%.

The thrust and torque are measured by a force transducer installed between the turbine rotor and the motor shaft (Extended Data Fig. 7). The transducer is bespoke, manufactured by Applied Measurements, rated for an axial load of 1,300 N and a torque of 100 N m, and a resolution of 0.005 N and 0.0004 N m, respectively. In this study, thrust is the net force measured by the hub transducer along the streamwise direction, and torque is the net edgewise moment about the hub axis. Moreover, each blade root was instrumented with a flapwise custom root-bending-moment sensor. Calibration matrices for each sensor were obtained in situ before the test by applying known weights at four points along the cantilever beam attached to the sensor. All force signals were transmitted to a National Instruments NI 9203 acquisition system through a slip ring. The load cells were zeroed without flow before each set of measurements. For each measurement, loads were recorded at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz for 300 s. Rotor angular velocity was measured using an inductive proximity sensor that emitted one pulse per blade pass (three pulses per revolution), enabling determination of the revolution period and computation of the angular velocity.

The principal measured quantities were torque (Q), thrust (T), flapwise root-bending moment (M) and angular velocity (ω). Measured loads and power are non-dimensionalized using standard turbine coefficients:

where ω is the turbine angular velocity in radians per second.

Sensor accuracy and calibration uncertainties were propagated to the non-dimensional coefficients using standard bias-limit uncertainty analysis32, including thrust-torque transducer manufacturer specification (0.1% of full-scale capacity) and primary uncertainties in u∞, ω and geometric parameters. For the present setup, the maximum total bias limits is of order 10−2 for CP and of order 10−2 for CT (representative values). Supplementary Note 1 provides the full derivations and tables.

Blade deformation was measured using phase-locked DIC with underwater cameras and LED illumination (LaVision). The camera system had a fixed focal length of 1.1 m and a field of view of approximately 0.87 m × 0.56 m, sufficient to capture the full blade span (0.56 m). Phase locking was achieved by using the proximity-sensor signal to trigger image acquisition as a blade passed a fixed azimuthal position, with a horizontal span and a downward tangential velocity. For each condition, between 89 and 447 instantaneous deformation fields were recorded over a 300 s period, depending on u∞ and λ.

Images were processed in LaVision DaVis 11 using a subset size of 21 × 21 pixels and a grid step size of 2 × 2 pixels, resulting in a spatial resolution of approximately 0.68 mm near the blade tip (approximately 2% of the tip chord). A reference image in quiescent water was acquired before each set of measurements. In the present configuration, DIC was used to measure the deformation of the suction-side surface of the blade. The full blade profile was reconstructed by combining the measured chord-line deformation with the known undeformed thickness distribution.

A bespoke fluid–structure interaction (FSI) solver was developed for the present study. The solver couples an in-house code based on blade element momentum theory (BEMT), with a panel method with an integral boundary-layer formulation (XFOIL), and a finite element analysis commercial software (Abaqus). The code uses a two-level iterative process, as schematically shown in Extended Data Fig. 9. The process begins with an initial blade geometry. In the outer loop, the BEMT solver is used to calculate the axial and tangential induction factors on a finite number of blade sections at different radial coordinates. Then, the flow velocity and angle of attack experienced by each blade section are computed. These values are used as initial conditions for the inner FSI loop. First, the pressure distributions around each blade section are computed with XFOIL. Then, the pressure distributions from each blade section are combined to obtain a three-dimensional pressure distribution on the blade, which is used as input to Abaqus, in which a new deformed shape is computed. The Abaqus model includes the steel spar. This new shape is then discretized into sections and returned to XFOIL to recalculate the pressure field. This iterative process continues until the blade shape converges. This deformed blade geometry at equilibrium is then fed back into the outer BEMT loop to update the induction factors. This entire two-level process is repeated until convergence. The power and thrust coefficients of the whole turbine are then computed by integrating the loads computed with XFOIL for each blade section and multiplying by three to account for the three-bladed turbine.

This code was used to design the stress-free mould shape for each blade stiffness, ensuring that the equilibrium blade shape matches the reference rigid blade at the design flow speed and tip-speed ratio. The model-scale simulations in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 are initialized with the mould geometry and use the actual stiffness of the metal spar and of the rubber. In the full-scale simulations (Extended Data Fig. 5), the stiffness of both the spar and the rubber is 10.6 times higher than at model scale to ensure that the model and full-scale Cauchy number for both the spar and the rubber is the same, where

where ρ is the fluid mass density and E is the Young’s modulus.

The mould geometry Xi,j is used as input, where i = 0 and j = 0 indicate the iteration number of the inner and outer loop, respectively. The lift and drag coefficient curves (\({C}_{{{\rm{L}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\), \({C}_{{{\rm{D}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\)) are computed with XFOIL for various blade sections, and the induction factors (\({a}_{i,j},{a}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\)) are computed with BEMT. Then the pressure distribution (pi,j(x)) around each blade section is computed with XFOIL and assembled into a three-dimensional load condition for Abaqus, where the new geometry is computed (Xi,j, with i increased by one). The inner loop is repeated till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi−1,j∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵi. If converged, the new geometry is Xi,j, where j is increased by one. The outer loop is repeated from the computation of the lift and drag coefficient for the new geometry, till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi,j−1∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵj.

#1919. How to watch Germany vs Netherlands: TV channel and live stream for Nations League today

The Standard's journalism is supported by our readers. If you click links to other sites on this page, we will earn commission.

Nations League fates will be decided this evening as Germany and the Netherlands face off in a mouth-watering showdown between two European heavyweights.

Both teams are largely in control of their own destiny, though a draw would certainly suit the Dutch more as it would be enough to top Group A2 and secure home advantage in the quarter-final second leg - which will be played in March 2027.

Germany, now managed by former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss Jurgen Klopp, can finish first but must beat the Netherlands and hope Greece fail to do so against a Serbia side that has lost all five matches thus far.

A point here for the Germans would leave qualification for the knockout phase hanging by a thread and they would be left relying on Serbia to beat Greece in Volos.

The reverse fixture between Germany and Netherlands finished all square in September as Cody Gakpo denied his former manager (Klopp) victory in his first game in charge of the national team with a 92nd minute equaliser in Amsterdam.

The Dutch have gone on to win three times since, including a 7-0 thumping of Greece on Friday night, but are without a win over Germany since September 2019.

Here’s everything you need to know about the Nations League, A2 clash...

Germany vs Netherlands is today, Monday, November 16, 2026, with kick-off at 7.45pm GMT.

The game will take place at the Olympiastadion, in Berlin.

TV channel and live stream: UK viewers can watch the game on Prime Video UK, who is the UK broadcaster for Nations League matches that do not involve England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.

Each game costs £2.49, and coverage begins around 10 minutes before kick-off.

#1916. Sarina Wiegman receives honorary damehood from Prince William at Windsor Castle - after leading Lionesses to back-to-back European titles

Published: 14:28 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 10 November 2026

Lionesses manager Sarina Wiegman has been awarded an honorary damehood by Prince William after leading England to back-to-back Euro wins.

Wiegman is Dutch and therefore cannot be made a substantive dame. Instead she has picked up the honorary title, because the Netherlands does not have a British monarch as its head of state.

She said upon being awarded the title at Windsor Castle on Tuesday: 'I feel very privileged to receive my honorary Damehood from His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle today.

'It is a day I will never forget and made even more special by sharing it with members of my family.

'I would like to again express my sincere gratitude for this honour and for the continued respect and warmth I experience from the English people. I thank everyone for their support.'

Wiegman was named in the King's New Year's Honours list at the end of 2025, alongside several members of her England team.

England manager Sarina Wiegman (left) has been awarded an honourary damehood by Prince William (right)

Captain Leah Williamson was awarded a CBE, with Alex Greenwood, Keira Walsh, Georgia Stanway and Ella Toone all being honoured with MBEs.

Wiegman said at the time: 'I would like to express my sincere gratitude for this honour. When I first arrived in England, I could never have imagined the respect and warmth I've experienced from the English people. I deeply thank the fans for their support.

'This title is a reflection of my exceptional team of players and staff. My congratulations go to Alex, Ella, Georgia, Keira, Leah and also Dr Ritan Mehta who have all been celebrated for their brilliant contributions.

'Our team values mean that when there is recognition for one, then there is recognition for all. I want to pay tribute to every member of our EURO squad. They should all be celebrated for everything they brought to the pitch and for the positive role they play in society. I'm proud to work alongside such a dedicated group of people.'

The former Netherlands coach took over the England team in 2021 and led them to success at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025.

She also reached the World Cup final in 2023, and signed a new two-year contract extension earlier this year, which will take her to the end of the 2029 Euros.

#1915. Who will England face in Nations League quarter-final? Next opponents confirmed after Spain win

England are on course to record their best ever performance in the Nations League, having qualified for the quarter-finals as group winners ahead of world champions Spain.

England player ratings: Surprise Arsenal star scores 8/10 as huge statement issued

Ice warnings in force with motorists urged to take care

How to watch Germany vs Netherlands: TV channel and live stream

Including its inaugural season in 2018/19, the Three Lions have competed in every single Nations League campaign, experiencing some highs and the lowest of lows.

From topping their group and qualifying for the Nations League finals and finishing third to suffering a shock relegation in 2022/23 and then immediate promotion, England have done almost everything except win the competition.

Having started the 2026/27 campaign with a loss to Spain, despite leading 2-1 at one stage, England bounced back in style by beating the Czechs twice and then thumping Croatia 7-0 in a remarkable, record-breaking rout.

Another win over Croatia followed at Wembley to confirm a top-two finish in the group and qualify for the Nations League knockout stage.

England then beat Spain in a one-game shootout in Madrid to win the group and with that, potentially securing, an easier quarter-final tie next March.

The four group winners will face the four runners-up in a two-legged Nations League quarter-final.

The group winners will all be seeded and will have home advantage in their respective second leg ties. Teams from the same group cannot be paired together in the knockout stage, therefore England and Spain - for example - will be kept apart.

As a result of finishing top in Group A3, England’s one confirmed potential Nations League quarter-final opponent so far is Belgium after they were pipped to top spot in Group A1 by France.

England’s remaining possible quarter-final opponents will be revealed over the next couple of nights, but as things currently stand, they could be drawn against either Greece or Denmark.

The draw for the 2026/27 Nations League quarter-final will take place on Friday, November 20 with the ties scheduled to take place in March 2027.

#1914. Prediction: USA vs Haiti

The United States head into Tuesday’s second leg of their CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final against Haiti with one foot already in the semi-finals.

After a dominant 6-0 victory in the opening meeting, it would take an extraordinary turnaround for the Americans to be eliminated, as Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his final match in charge before departing for Manchester United.

The USA have little left to do but finish the tie professionally after dismantling Haiti in the first leg.

Tuesday’s match will represent the final game of Mauricio Pochettino’s tenure, and the Argentine will be eager to leave on a high note. While he departs without delivering silverware, he has overseen significant progress since the World Cup, with the United States currently riding a five-match winning streak in all competitions.

The Americans have been particularly impressive in recent months, keeping three consecutive clean sheets and scoring at least three goals in four of their last five matches.

Home form has also been a major strength. The USA have a perfect record in Nations League quarter-final matches on home soil and remain unbeaten at TQL Stadium, where they have won two previous internationals.

History is also firmly on their side. The United States are unbeaten in their last 11 meetings with Haiti and have won the last four encounters by an aggregate score of 10-1.

Julian Hall was the youngest player in the American starting lineup during the first leg, while Santiago Castaneda and Reed Baker-Whiting are still waiting to make their senior international debuts.

Christian Pulisic and Weston McKennie both made their first appearances since the World Cup in the opening match of the tie and immediately made an impact. Pulisic scored twice, while McKennie also found the net.

Hall, Auston Trusty and Folarin Balogun were also on the scoresheet as the Americans ran riot.

Haiti travel to Cincinnati facing a seemingly impossible task after suffering a crushing defeat in the first leg.

David Badia’s side had entered the quarter-finals with momentum after winning their opening three Nations League group-stage matches, but back-to-back defeats have abruptly halted that progress. Their last two losses have come by a combined score of 8-0.

The 6-0 defeat to the USA was particularly painful, marking the first time since 2021 that Haiti had conceded six goals in a single match.

Despite the deficit, Haiti will still be determined to finish the campaign with a positive performance. Their last quarter-final victory in a CONCACAF competition came during the 2019 Gold Cup, when they staged a remarkable comeback from 2-0 down to beat Canada 3-2.

The visitors are also attempting to secure their first victory on American soil against the United States since a World Cup qualifier triumph in 1969.

Goalkeeper Jonah Mednard and midfielder Miguel Joseph remain uncapped at senior international level.

Fabrice Picault is pushing for a place in the starting lineup after beginning the first leg on the bench, while Ruben Providence and Yassin Fortune could also be considered for greater involvement.

With a six-goal advantage already established, the United States can approach this fixture with confidence and relatively little pressure. Pochettino’s side have been in excellent form, while Haiti appear to have lost momentum at exactly the wrong time.

Even if the Americans rotate heavily, the gulf in quality and confidence between the teams should still be evident. Haiti may offer greater resistance than in the first leg, but another comfortable home victory looks the most likely outcome.

#1913. England: How many games Elliot Anderson will miss after Spain red card

Elliot Anderson is facing a suspension after being sent-off in England’s Nations League win over Spain.

Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White had the Three Lions cruising to victory at 3-0 on Sunday night, before Anderson’s challenge on Lamine Yamal produced both a red card and a penalty.

Mikel Oyarzabal successfully converted the spot-kick before substitute Nico Williams reduced deficit with 15 minutes plus stoppage time remaining.

Ultimately, England held on for a famous win and topped Group A3 as a result.

England will discover their quarter-final opponents later this week, but they will be without Anderson for the first-leg because of the red card.

UEFA rules stipulate “a player or team official sent off by the referee is automatically suspended for the next match in the competition.

“In the event of a serious offence, the UEFA disciplinary bodies are entitled to augment this punishment, including by extending it to other competitions.”

Due to Anderson being given his marching orders in the Spanish capital for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity, rather than violent conduct, his punishment will be a one-game ban.

Therefore, the Manchester City midfielder will be available for the second leg in March 2027 - if named in the England squad by Thomas Tuchel.

Tuchel, meanwhile, slammed the decision as a ‘double punishment’ during his post-match press conference, dissecting a classic England performance after becoming the first team to beat Spain in 43 competitive matches.

Tuchel commented: “The red card and the penalty is always a big decision - and I need to understand why it's a double punishment.

"Then it was a long, long 30 minutes - but I don't want to focus on that. There was so, so many positive things about the result after 60 minutes. It was well deserved.”

The England manager also made reference to his side’s performance with 10 men during the World Cup, when the Three Lions held on after a red card against hosts Mexico to win 3-2 in the round of 16.

"For me, the red card was more like the Azteca reloaded,” continued Tuchel.

"Against this team half an hour feels like two hours. Full of quality. You can see the second goal coming and it's a long, long time to overcome it. That's the way it is.

"We showed that without the red card, we had a clear win. Brilliant performance overall. We were the better team. We put out a fantastic performance from start to finish.”

#1912. ‘Exposed the world champions’: Spanish press react to England win in Nations League

10 man England secured a miraculous 3-2 win against world champions Spain in Madrid to top their Nations League group.

The Three Lions raced into a 3-0 lead at the Metropolitano Stadium, before Elliot Anderson conceded a penalty and was shown a straight red card for bringing down Lamine Yamal inside the area.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored the resulting spot-kick, and substitute Nico Williams set up a nervy finish as he slotted the ball home after a quick counter-attack.

Despite late pressure from Spain, England held on thanks to a superb double save from James Trafford, ending La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run on a memorable night for Thomas Tuchel’s side.

Sunday’s result will go down as one of the most remarkable nights in England’s recent history, with Tuchel admitting his team reached the “highest level football-wise in all aspects of the game”.

Meanwhile, captain Harry Kane, who opened the scoring from the penalty spot at the end of the first half, said the victory was “as big as it gets” outside of a major tournament.

England entered the international break still carrying the scars of the World Cup, with Tuchel facing significant criticism for his in-game management during their semi-final defeat to Argentina.

However, victory over Spain means England have now won five of their six matches since returning from America, while Tuchel can point to having got his substitutions right as his side held on with 10 men to beat the reigning world and European champions in their own backyard.

England made the perfect start in the Spanish capital, with Declan Rice claiming post-match that, “The first 10 minutes was the best we’ve played” as Luis de La Fuente’s side struggled to live with England’s pressing.

ITV pundit and former Manchester United midfielder Roy Keane was similarly impressed by England’s intense start, describing their first-half performance as “perfect” after Kane gave the visitors a deserved lead just before the break.

Keane’s ITV colleague, Ian Wright, was particularly pleased for Arsenal right-back Ben White, who was subjected to boos during England’s 2-1 victory over Croatia but started and scored against Spain after a flowing passing move.

“Can I just say, I’m really pleased for Ben White and the way things have turned around for him. It’s just brilliant for him to get back in, and he was magnificent tonight,” Wright said.

“Not just with the goal, but he was making tackles, niggling the Spain players. I’m so pleased it’s ended that way for him.

“There was a lot to be excited about for England. They were 3-0 up and cruising against the world champions before the red kind of changed the game.”

Spanish outlet AS also heaped praise on England’s performance, declaring the result as “the biggest setback of the De la Fuente era” with Tuchel’s men “completely neutralising Spain.”

“England exposed the world champions in what represents the biggest setback of the De la Fuente era, a bitter end to a dream 2026. Goals from Kane, Konsa, and White rewarded a superior opponent,” a report in AS stated.

“Tuchel’s men had managed to cut off both of their opponents’ cables, the red and the blue, completely neutralising Spain.”

England exposed the world champions in what represents the biggest setback of the De la Fuente era

Fellow Spanish outlet MARCA also chose to celebrate England’s dominance rather than attack Spain’s performance.

“It’s better to lose against a formidable opponent like England, who dominated the match until they were reduced to ten men,” MARCA said before continuing by lavishing praise on Tuchel.

“Credit goes to Tuchel, though his performance has been questioned because he seemed afraid to be the hero in the World Cup match against Argentina. It’s been a long time since an opponent has so thoroughly dismantled Spain.”

#1910. Scott McTominay reveals hospital dash and heart shock treatment days before Scotland's World Cup opener

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:25 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Scott McTominay has revealed he needed a procedure to reset the beat of his heart just two days before Scotland’s World Cup campaign kicked off back in June.

Heading into the opening game against Haiti in Boston, the explanation given from the Scottish Football Association was that McTominay had been carrying a sickness bug.

But, after the squad had flown from their training base in Charlotte, McTominay had actually been whisked away to hospital straight from the airport via a police escort.

The 29-year-old had shock treatment on his heart before then going on to play all three games as Steve Clarke’s side were knocked out at the group stage.

The Napoli midfielder subsequently underwent corrective surgery back at the start of the season and missed Scotland’s opening four fixtures in the Nations League.

Now back in the squad ahead of the upcoming double-header with North Macedonia and Switzerland, McTominay has opened up for the first time on his health issues.

Scott McTominay had a heart procedure two days before playing against Haiti

Scott McTominay in action during Scotland's 1-0 World Cup win over Haiti

Asked about what happened, he replied: ‘The sickness bug? You’re not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup. It’s not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before — well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup.

‘But you have to take the cards you’re dealt on the chin. It’s part of the game. There’s nothing I could do about it and the shock went well, I was back in normal rhythm then 24 hours later you’re playing a World Cup game.

‘The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game.

‘You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking: “How has this happened to me?” But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football.

‘Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say: “Well, it’s part of the process”.

McTominay was given full reassurance from the doctors and medical staff that the procedure had gone well, insisting it was never in his thoughts to pull out of the squad.

Asked whether it was playing on his mind across the three games against Haiti, Morocco and Brazil, he said: ‘No. I put it to bed. I tried my best to put it to bed anyway. Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and sleep and stuff like that.

‘You have to get back round to doing it again. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you’re dealt, there’s nothing you can do about it.’

Some fans had questioned McTominay’s form throughout the World Cup, oblivious to the fact that he was effectively playing through an ongoing heart issue.

Asked whether the criticism bothered him at the time, he continued: ‘It’s tough. It’s never easy, things like that, but you can’t use things like that as an excuse because that’s just not in my nature.

‘I take whole responsibility for a lot of the things that we didn’t create or didn’t score the goals in the World Cup.

‘I can put my face out there and say that that was nowhere near good enough. But that’s part of football. You have to get away and think about it and reflect and come back a better player.

‘I didn’t know that’s what people were saying. I probably had an idea.

‘I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it. You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be.

‘For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.’

#1909. England winners and losers: Arsenal star rebuilding as Chelsea man suffers further setback

A terrific week for England ended with an away victory over Spain which Thomas Tuchel described as “like the Azteca reloaded”.

The Three Lions closed out their 2026 campaign by finishing top of their Nations League group thanks to a 2-1 win over Croatia last Thursday and then a heroic 10-man win in Madrid, 3-2, on Sunday.

While plenty of Tuchel’s players pushed their cases for further England involvement down the line, there were others who will feel less positive about the past week in terms of what it means for them.

Here, Standard Sport considers the winners and losers from England’s impressive autumn week.

Ben White has scored only 12 goals in his senior career but two have been for England, including the eventual winner in a famous win in Madrid.

Five years after his England debut, his first competitive start for his country came in Spain, and he didn’t disappoint.

The Arsenal man followed up a cameo against Croatia with one of England’s standout performances at the Estadio Metropolitano, defending robustly against Spain’s attacks down the left and then chipping in with that overlapping run and finish to make it 3-0.

Has had to field booing from sections of England fans since his return to the international fold in March after he walked away from their World Cup squad in 2022, but is rebuilding his England career successfully and will be thought of by Tuchel as one of his most well-balanced right-back options now.

Hopes to climb above Reece James and become first choice.

England’s left-back position changed hands a few times during the World Cup as Nico O’Reilly and Djed Spence battled it out mid-tournament, but that only served to make Tuchel’s decision to leave Hall behind appear all the more strange.

Hall has come back stronger and this month backed up his encouraging displays from the last international break.

Solid in the 2-1 win over Croatia, he was on another level entirely in Madrid, taking care of the threat of Lamine Yamal and finding a perfect balance between defence and attack as he helped England to victory in the world champions’ own backyard.

At the end of the last international break, when Trafford and Jordan Pickford split the four games two each, Pickford could no longer claim to be uncontested as England No1.

And after his heroics in Spain, even more so there is a debate to be had over whether it is time for England’s first-choice goalkeeper to be Leeds United’s Trafford rather than his Everton counterpart.

De La Fuente makes Spain claim after Nations League defeat to England

Arsenal star confronted as tempers flare during Spain vs England

When is Nations League draw? Start time, quarter-final pots and TV

Winter escapes and activities to end the year in style

Pickford has never let England down in 94 caps, but Trafford made a string of stellar saves in Madrid and is eight years his junior.

Tuchel will likely continue to share the game time between them until he is pulled strongly enough in either direction. Trafford is making a very strong case for Pickford’s nine years without a genuine challenger to end with the shirt changing hands.

The Bayer Leverkusen defender has become accustomed to the bulk of his England game time being at right-back during this calendar year, but a shortage of centre-back options this month saw him start in the middle in both games

Quansah was solid for the most part but switched off in both games. And both errors were punished.

First he attempted a header back to Pickford from a Croatia corner that gifted the visitors a leveller at Wembley, then he dawdled on the ball long enough for Spain to intercept and race through; Elliot Anderson’s last-man red card and a Spain penalty followed.

Tuchel will hope he is stronger for the mistakes he made, but 23-year-old Quansah will be disappointed as he heads back to Germany.

Arguably it is harsh to include a player who was not even involved in the two matches, but the reason for Cole Palmer’s absence this month spoke volumes.

After dropping out of the last camp due to load management and being told by Tuchel that he “misses too many opportunities” to play for his country, this time the Chelsea talisman was not even selected.

Already faces huge competition in the No10 role but now there seems to be something of a repair job required if he is to get back into the fold and into Tuchel’s plans.

The 28-year-old is approaching 40 caps but his England career has been a strange old saga, really. Only Lee Carsley has ever appeared to truly trust him; Gareth Southgate and now Tuchel, less so.

Not in favour at Real Madrid under Jose Mourinho, his England game time across the autumn has felt a result of Reece James’s injuries and evidence right-back is a problem position more than it has an opportunity earned through strong club form.

Categorising Alexander-Arnold as a sublime passer who is suspect defensively became cliché long ago — yet being pinched of the ball in a poor area by Croatia was just the latest confirmation.

England managers have lacked the faith required to start him in England’s toughest matches for years now, and so it continued as he remained an unused substitute in Madrid.

White is just the latest player to climb above him in the pecking order.

#1908. Everton set sights on Samuel Lino

According to the Liverpool Echo, Everton have identified Samuel Lino as a potential transfer target as the club looks to strengthen its options on the wing. The Brazilian has been in excellent form for Flamengo, contributing 21 goals and assists in 33 league appearances this season.

Everton are believed to be assessing the wide areas of their squad amid uncertainty surrounding the long-term future of Jack Grealish. While youngster Tyrique George has been trusted on the left flank in recent matches, the club may be keen to add experience and competition for places rather than rely solely on the 20-year-old.

Lino’s attacking output has made him one of Flamengo’s standout performers under Leonardo Jardim. He has played a major role for the Brazilian giants, ranking among the squad leaders for minutes played while also emerging as the team’s top assist provider.

The 26-year-old already has significant European experience. During his time at Atletico Madrid, he made 93 appearances under Diego Simeone between 2023 and 2025, while he has also earned four senior caps for Brazil.

#1907. GdS: The ‘dream’ and two alternatives – Milan draw up three-man centre-back wish list

AC Milan are in the market for a new central defender ahead of the winter window, and three names are on the list.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below), Gerry Cardinale wants to give Ruben Amorim at least two signings in January. One of them will be a centre-forward – with Nicolo Tresoldi the ambitious idea at the moment – while the other will be a defender.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

With Matteo Gabbia sidelined until well into January and Fikayo Tomori currently injured, Amorim has been juggling an emergency in recent weeks. It was a situation further compounded by an issue that arose for Strahinja Pavlović last week.

Fortunately for Amorim, he has found a capable alternative in the youngster Sankhoun Diawara. Looking ahead, however, the club is considering an addition that could immediately boost the level of the department.

A summer target was Gonçalo Inácio whom Amorim knows well, having coached him for years at Sporting CP. Dialogue with the Lisbon club has continued even during the current period when the transfer window is closed, following the failure to reach an agreement before.

Milan could renew their pursuit soon, though there is currently no consensus regarding his asking price. Furthermore, Inácio is left-footed and has primarily played as an outside centre-back throughout his career.

What the Rossoneri need right now is more of a right-footed player capable of rotating between a wide centre-back role and a central position. While it is true that Gonçalo adapted to the right side under Amorim, there are other candidates who are a more natural fit for that role.

For instance, Ismaelo Ganiou of RC Lens has been on the radar for some time. His contract renewal in August does not necessarily rule out a transfer, although there has been no further contact with the French club since initial discussions in the summer.

Among the new names, 21-year-old Massiré Sylla of Union Saint-Gilloise is an intriguing prospect. The Belgian club have also moved quickly to secure their young star with a new contract until 2031. That said, it is not a major obstacle, and the price is around €15m.
